questions.q: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify chargeability to profits tax where no return has been issued?
options: 4 months after the end of the basis period
1 month after the end of the basis period
3 months after the end of the basis period
6 months after the end of the basis period
questions.explain: A person chargeable to tax who has not received a return must notify the Commissioner in writing within 4 months after the end of the basis period for the year of assessment concerned.

questions.q: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify the commencement of an employee's employment?
options: 1 month after the date of commencement
3 months after the date of commencement
2 months after the date of commencement
before the employee starts work
questions.explain: An employer must file Form IR56E within 3 months of employing anyone likely to be chargeable to salaries tax.

questions.q: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify the cessation of an employee's employment?
options: 3 months after the date of cessation
1 month after the date of cessation
1 month before the date of cessation
within 14 days of the date of cessation
questions.explain: Form IR56F is due not later than 1 month before the employee ceases to be employed.

questions.q: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify that an employee is about to leave Hong Kong permanently?
options: 1 month after the date of departure
3 months before the expected date of departure
on the date of departure
1 month before the expected date of departure
questions.explain: Form IR56G must be filed not later than 1 month before the expected date of departure. This is the obligation the June 2026 examining team reported candidates most often missed.

questions.q: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify a change of the taxpayer's postal address?
options: 1 month after the change
3 months after the change
before the change takes effect
at the time the next return is filed
questions.explain: Any person chargeable who changes address must inform the Commissioner in writing within 1 month.

questions.q: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer apply for business registration after commencing business?
options: 3 months after commencement
1 month after commencement
before commencement
4 months after the end of the first basis period
questions.explain: Business registration must be applied for within 1 month of commencing business, separately from the s.51(2) notification of chargeability.

questions.q: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer lodge a valid notice of objection against an assessment?
options: 1 month after the end of the year of assessment
2 months after the date of the notice of assessment
1 month after the date of the notice of assessment
6 months after the date of the notice of assessment
questions.explain: An objection must be lodged in writing within 1 month of the date of the notice of assessment, and must state the precise grounds.

questions.q: Within what period must a taxpayer or employer appeal to the Board of Review against the Commissioner's determination?
options: 14 days after the determination
2 months after the determination
3 months after the determination
1 month after the determination is transmitted
questions.explain: An appeal to the Board of Review must be lodged within 1 month of the Commissioner's written determination.

questions.q: For how long must a person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong retain sufficient business records?
options: 7 years
5 years
6 years
10 years
questions.explain: Section 51C requires records sufficient to enable assessable profits to be readily ascertained to be kept for at least 7 years after the transaction. Failure carries a fine at level 6.

questions.q: From what point does the statutory retention period for business records run?
options: 7 years after the end of the year of assessment
7 years after the transaction to which they relate
6 years after the transaction
Until the assessment for that year becomes final and conclusive
questions.explain: The period runs for 7 years from the completion of the transaction, not from the year end or the date of assessment.

questions.q: A landlord letting a Hong Kong property is obliged to keep rental records. What must those records cover?
options: Only the tenancy agreement
Only bank statements showing rent received
Rent records, and records of rates and any irrecoverable rent
No records are required for property income
questions.explain: Records must be sufficient to establish the assessable value: rent receivable, any premium, rates paid by the owner, and any rent treated as irrecoverable. June 2026 candidates could state the 7-year period but not what had to be kept.

questions.q: Within what period may the Assessor normally raise an additional assessment where income has been under-assessed?
options: 4 years from the end of the year of assessment
7 years from the end of the year of assessment
There is no time limit
6 years from the end of the year of assessment
questions.explain: Six years from the end of the relevant year of assessment, extended to 10 years in a case of fraud or wilful evasion.

questions.q: Where a taxpayer has been guilty of fraud or wilful evasion, within what period may an additional assessment be raised?
options: 10 years
6 years
12 years
No limit applies
questions.explain: The ordinary 6-year limit is extended to 10 years.

questions.q: A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $11,250. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?
questions.explain: Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $11,250) = $43,750. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

questions.q: A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $24,000. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?
questions.explain: Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $24,000) = $82,000. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

questions.q: A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $8,400. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?
questions.explain: Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $8,400) = $35,200. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

questions.q: A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $46,500. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?
questions.explain: Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $46,500) = $149,500. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

questions.q: What is the maximum additional tax the Commissioner may assess under s.82A for an incorrect return made without reasonable excuse?
options: A fine of $10,000 only
Additional tax not exceeding treble the amount undercharged
Imprisonment for up to 3 years
A surcharge of 5% of the tax undercharged
questions.explain: Section 82A is an administrative penalty - no criminal intent need be proved - of up to treble the tax undercharged. It is assessed by the Commissioner, in place of prosecution.

questions.q: What is the maximum penalty for wilfully and with intent evading tax, on conviction on indictment?
options: A fine of $10,000 and imprisonment for 6 months
Additional tax of treble the amount undercharged only
A fine of treble the tax undercharged and imprisonment for 3 years
A surcharge of 15.5% of the tax
questions.explain: Section 82 is the criminal provision: a fine of treble the tax undercharged plus imprisonment for up to 3 years. Distinguish it from s.82A, which is administrative and carries no imprisonment.

questions.q: Tax of $100,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?
questions.explain: A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($5,000), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($10,500), giving $115,500. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

questions.q: Tax of $48,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?
questions.explain: A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($2,400), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($5,040), giving $55,440. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

questions.q: Tax of $250,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?
questions.explain: A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($12,500), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($26,250), giving $288,750. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

questions.q: A demand note is payable in two instalments and the taxpayer misses the first. What is the consequence?
options: Only the unpaid first instalment attracts the 5% surcharge
The surcharge is deferred until the second instalment falls due
The second instalment becomes immediately due and the 5% surcharge applies to the whole outstanding balance
No surcharge arises until 6 months after the second due date
questions.explain: Missing the first instalment accelerates the second, and the 5% surcharge is imposed on the entire outstanding balance - not merely on the instalment that was missed.

questions.q: A taxpayer in financial difficulty applies successfully to pay tax by instalments. What is the effect on surcharges?
options: Surcharges are waived once the arrangement is approved
Surcharges are halved
Surcharges are deferred until the final instalment
Surcharges are still imposed on tax unpaid after the due date
questions.explain: IRD is explicit that an approved instalment arrangement does not stop the surcharge. It buys time and heads off recovery action; it is not a waiver.

questions.q: Under which provision may the Commissioner issue a recovery notice to a third party who owes money to the defaulter?
options: s.82A
questions.explain: A recovery notice under s.76 may be served on an employer, bank, tenant, debtor or customer, requiring them to pay the money to IRD instead.

questions.q: Under which provision may the Commissioner apply to a District Judge to stop a defaulter leaving Hong Kong?
questions.explain: A departure prevention direction under s.77 lasts until the tax is paid or security is given.

questions.q: Under which provision may the Commissioner sue for tax in default as a civil debt in the District Court?
questions.explain: Tax in default is recoverable as a civil debt, with the usual consequences of judgment including costs.

questions.q: Four people own a let property as co-owners in equal shares. How are they liable for the property tax?
options: Severally only - each owner is liable for their own share
Jointly only - all owners must be sued together
Only the owner named first on the demand note is liable
Jointly and severally - any one owner may be pursued for the whole
questions.explain: Liability is joint and several: IRD may pursue any one co-owner for the whole amount, not merely their quarter share. Once one pays in full, recovery against the others stops and tax is never collected twice.

questions.q: By when must an application to hold over payment of provisional tax be made?
options: Not later than 28 days before the due date, or 14 days after the notice is issued, whichever is later
Not later than 14 days before the due date
At any time before the end of the year of assessment
Within 1 month of the notice being issued
questions.explain: The later of 28 days before the due date and 14 days after the notice. The grounds are prescribed - for instance a fall in income of more than 10%, cessation, or an election for personal assessment.

questions.q: Which of the following is a valid statutory ground for holding over provisional salaries tax?
options: The taxpayer expects a lower salary next year
Assessable income for the year is likely to be less than 90% of that of the preceding year
The taxpayer has already paid the first instalment
The taxpayer objects to the amount of the provisional tax
questions.explain: A fall to below 90% of the preceding year's assessable income is one of the prescribed grounds. Mere disagreement with the amount is not.

questions.q: What may the Assessor issue where a taxpayer fails to file a return?
options: No assessment until the return is filed
An automatic penalty of treble the tax
An estimated assessment based on the best information available
A referral to the Board of Review
questions.explain: An estimated assessment under s.59(3). It protects the statutory time limit and is superseded once the actual figures are agreed, usually through an objection.

questions.q: What happens to the tax in dispute while an objection is under consideration?
options: It is automatically suspended until the objection is determined
Half the tax must be paid and half is suspended
The Commissioner must always accept security instead
It is not automatically suspended; a separate holdover application is needed
questions.explain: Lodging an objection does not suspend the tax. The taxpayer must separately apply to hold over the disputed portion, and the Commissioner may require security or purchase of a Tax Reserve Certificate.

questions.q: A notice of objection is lodged in time but states no grounds. What is the consequence?
options: It may be rejected as invalid
It is treated as valid but given lower priority
The Assessor must request further particulars before rejecting it
It automatically becomes an appeal to the Board of Review
questions.explain: An objection must state the precise grounds. A bare, unparticularised objection can be rejected as invalid even though it was lodged within the month.

questions.q: What is the status of a DIPN?
options: DIPNs have the force of law
Departmental Interpretation and Practice Notes are not binding on taxpayers or the courts
DIPNs bind the taxpayer but not the Commissioner
DIPNs override the Inland Revenue Ordinance where they conflict
questions.explain: DIPNs explain how IRD interprets and administers the law. They bind nobody - a taxpayer may object to a treatment set out in one. In the hierarchy of authority they sit below statute, case law and Board of Review decisions.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly ranks the authority of Hong Kong tax sources, highest first?
options: DIPNs, then statute, then case law
Advance rulings, then DIPNs, then statute
Statute, then case law, then Board of Review decisions, then DIPNs, then advance rulings
Case law, then statute, then DIPNs
questions.explain: Statute is supreme, followed by subsidiary legislation and case law, then Board of Review decisions, then DIPNs, with advance rulings least persuasive because they turn on their own facts.

questions.q: What distinguishes tax avoidance from tax evasion?
options: They are the same thing
Avoidance is illegal; evasion is lawful
Avoidance applies to companies and evasion to individuals
Tax avoidance uses lawful means; tax evasion is illegal
questions.explain: Avoidance arranges affairs lawfully to reduce tax; evasion involves deceit, concealment or false statements and is criminal. Note that general and specific anti-avoidance provisions are excluded from the TX-HKG syllabus.

questions.q: What is the effect of a specific advance ruling issued by the Commissioner?
options: A ruling applies only to the applicant and the arrangement described
A ruling binds all taxpayers in a similar position
A ruling is published and may be relied on by anyone
A ruling is binding on the courts
questions.explain: A specific ruling may be relied on only by the applicant, and only for the arrangement and period described. Published versions are anonymised and are persuasive at best.

questions.q: Who is empowered to assess and collect tax under the Inland Revenue Ordinance?
options: The Financial Secretary
The Commissioner
The Chief Executive
The Board of Review
questions.explain: The Commissioner of Inland Revenue, who is also Collector of Stamp Revenue and Commissioner of Estate Duty.

questions.q: What is the Board of Review?
options: A division of the Inland Revenue Department
A committee of the Legislative Council
An independent statutory body that hears tax appeals
A branch of the District Court
questions.explain: An independent statutory body constituted under s.65, with a chairman, deputy chairmen with legal training, and up to 150 members appointed by the Chief Executive. It hears appeals against the Commissioner's determinations.

questions.q: On what basis may a Board of Review decision be appealed to the Court of First Instance by way of case stated?
options: Any question of fact or law
Questions of fact only
Only the amount of the assessment
A point of law only
questions.explain: The Board is the final arbiter of fact. An appeal by case stated under s.69 lies on a question of law only.

questions.q: For 2025/26 profits tax returns with Accounting Date Code 'D', what were the extended lodgement dates announced by the Commissioner on 14 July 2026?
options: 31 August 2026 for paper filing and 2 October 2026 for electronic
17 August 2026 and 17 September 2026 respectively
30 April 2026 and 31 May 2026 respectively
There is no extension for 'D' code returns
questions.explain: Code 'D' covers accounting dates from 1 to 31 December. The paper deadline moved from 17 August to 31 August 2026, and the electronic deadline from 17 September to 2 October 2026. Codes 'N' and 'M' were unchanged.

questions.q: When is a newly incorporated Hong Kong company normally issued with its first profits tax return?
options: Within 1 month of incorporation
Around 18 months after incorporation or commencement of business
Within 4 months of the first year end
Only after the company notifies chargeability
questions.explain: Usually about 18 months after incorporation or commencement. The company must still notify chargeability under s.51(2) within 4 months of the basis period end if no return has arrived by then.

questions.q: Besides simply processing what a return states, what compliance activity does the Inland Revenue Department carry out?
options: IRD only ever reviews a return if the taxpayer itself requests it
Every return is manually checked line by line before assessment
Field assessments/audits, and desk audits and field investigations into offshore claims and transfer pricing risk
Reviews are limited to companies with a history of late filing
questions.explain: IRD runs a risk-based programme of field audits and investigations - including into offshore profits claims and transfer pricing - as well as desk-based reviews, quite separately from the routine processing of assessments.

questions.q: What must generally accompany the first return filed by a newly registered taxpayer, in addition to the return itself?
options: A passport is always sufficient on its own
No form of identification is ever required to file a return
Only a bank statement is required
A Hong Kong identity card, or - for a company - its certificate of incorporation and business registration certificate, plus supporting documents as requested
questions.explain: Basic identification and registration documents - an HKID for an individual, or the certificate of incorporation and business registration certificate for a company - together with any supporting schedules IRD specifically requests.

questions.q: Under the totality of facts test in Goepfert, which three factors principally determine whether an employment is a Hong Kong employment?
options: Where the contract was negotiated and is enforceable, the residence of the employer, and where remuneration is paid
Where the employee lives, works and banks
The nationality of the employee and the employer
Where the employment was advertised and where tax is withheld
questions.explain: The three Goepfert factors. They are indicative, not conclusive - the test is the totality of the facts (DIPN 10).

questions.q: Income from services rendered wholly outside Hong Kong by a non-Government employee is excluded from salaries tax unless the person visited Hong Kong for what period during the basis period?
options: 60 days or more
More than 60 days
More than 90 days
More than 183 days
questions.explain: Section 8(1B) brings the visit days back into charge where the person was in Hong Kong for more than 60 days. It is a cliff edge: 61 days loses the whole exemption, and both the arrival and departure day count in full, even for a same-day transit.

questions.q: An employee's ordinary visits to Hong Kong total 59 days. On two occasions he also departed very early in the morning on a connecting flight. How many days does he count as present?
questions.explain: Both the day of arrival and the day of departure count as a full day each, even for a same-day transit. 59 + 2 = 61, which exceeds 60, so the s.8(1B) exemption fails entirely.

questions.q: An employee has a Hong Kong employment with a company managed and controlled in Hong Kong. He spent 9 months working in a territory with no double taxation arrangement with Hong Kong, and that salary bore local income tax of $180,000, which the employer paid on his behalf. His salary is $100,000 a month. What is his assessable income?
questions.explain: Section 8(1A)(c) excludes income for services rendered in a non-DTA territory where tax of substantially the same nature has been paid there, so the 9 months' salary drops out. But foreign tax borne by the employer is itself a taxable perquisite: ($100,000 × 3) + $180,000 = $480,000. Omitting the employer-paid tax is the commonest error.

questions.q: An employee has a Hong Kong employment with a company managed and controlled in Hong Kong. He spent 10 months working in a territory with no double taxation arrangement with Hong Kong, and that salary bore local income tax of $250,000, which the employer paid on his behalf. His salary is $120,000 a month. What is his assessable income?
questions.explain: Section 8(1A)(c) excludes income for services rendered in a non-DTA territory where tax of substantially the same nature has been paid there, so the 10 months' salary drops out. But foreign tax borne by the employer is itself a taxable perquisite: ($120,000 × 2) + $250,000 = $490,000. Omitting the employer-paid tax is the commonest error.

questions.q: An employee has a Hong Kong employment with a company managed and controlled in Hong Kong. He spent 8 months working in a territory with no double taxation arrangement with Hong Kong, and that salary bore local income tax of $150,000, which the employer paid on his behalf. His salary is $80,000 a month. What is his assessable income?
questions.explain: Section 8(1A)(c) excludes income for services rendered in a non-DTA territory where tax of substantially the same nature has been paid there, so the 8 months' salary drops out. But foreign tax borne by the employer is itself a taxable perquisite: ($80,000 × 4) + $150,000 = $470,000. Omitting the employer-paid tax is the commonest error.

questions.q: How are directors' fees from a company resident in Hong Kong treated?
options: Sourced where the director physically performs the duties
Exempt if the director spends fewer than 60 days in Hong Kong
Always Hong Kong sourced, wherever the services are rendered
Apportioned by time spent in Hong Kong
questions.explain: A directorship is located where the company is centrally managed and controlled, so the fees are fully Hong Kong sourced regardless of where the director works. Time apportionment and the 60-day rule do not apply.

questions.q: An employee's income after allowable outgoings is $998,000. The employer provides a self-contained flat rent free, at a cost to the employer of $240,000 for the year. What rental value is assessable?
questions.explain: Rental value is a percentage of income after s.12(1)(a) outgoings: 10% for a flat or other self-contained accommodation, 8% for two rooms in a hotel, hostel or boarding house, and 4% for a single room. Here $998,000 × 10% = $99,800.

questions.q: An employee's income after allowable outgoings is $600,000. The employer provides two rooms in a hotel rent free, at a cost to the employer of $156,000 for the year. What rental value is assessable?
questions.explain: Rental value is a percentage of income after s.12(1)(a) outgoings: 10% for a flat or other self-contained accommodation, 8% for two rooms in a hotel, hostel or boarding house, and 4% for a single room. Here $600,000 × 8% = $48,000.

questions.q: An employee's income after allowable outgoings is $750,000. The employer provides a single hotel room rent free, at a cost to the employer of $132,000 for the year. What rental value is assessable?
questions.explain: Rental value is a percentage of income after s.12(1)(a) outgoings: 10% for a flat or other self-contained accommodation, 8% for two rooms in a hotel, hostel or boarding house, and 4% for a single room. Here $750,000 × 4% = $30,000.

questions.q: An employee's income after allowable outgoings is $1,200,000. The employer provides a rent-free house rent free, at a cost to the employer of $420,000 for the year. What rental value is assessable?
questions.explain: Rental value is a percentage of income after s.12(1)(a) outgoings: 10% for a flat or other self-contained accommodation, 8% for two rooms in a hotel, hostel or boarding house, and 4% for a single room. Here $1,200,000 × 10% = $120,000.

questions.q: An employee pays part of the rent on employer-provided quarters. How is the 'rent suffered' treated?
options: It is deducted from assessable income before the rental value is computed
It has no effect on the computation
It may create a negative rental value carried forward
It is deducted from the rental value, but only down to nil
questions.explain: Rent paid by the employee, less any rent refunded, reduces the rental value - but only to nil. It cannot create a negative figure or a loss.

questions.q: On what base is the 10% rental value calculated?
options: 10% of income after deducting the professional subscription
10% of gross salary before any deduction
10% of income after all concessionary deductions
10% of net chargeable income after allowances
questions.explain: Income after s.12(1)(a) outgoings but before self-education and the concessionary deductions. Using gross salary, or income after concessionary deductions, both give the wrong figure.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
Medical expenses reimbursed by the employer
options: Not assessable
Assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the cost
questions.explain: Reimbursement of an employee's own liability is assessable income. The June 2026 report names failing to assess it as a common error.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
Shipping costs and air fares paid by the employer to relocate a new employee and family to Hong Kong
options: Assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Not assessable
Assessable only at 50% of the cost
questions.explain: Genuine relocation expenses are not assessable - they are incurred for the employer's purposes, not as a reward for services.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
Interest saved on an interest-free loan from the employer
options: Assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the cost
Not assessable
questions.explain: A benefit that is not convertible into money and does not discharge the employee's own liability is outside the charge.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
A holiday journey paid for by the employer
options: Assessable
Not assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the cost
questions.explain: Section 9(2A)(c) assesses holiday journey benefits on the actual cost to the employer, whether or not convertible, apportioned for business-cum-holiday travel (DIPN 41).

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
The employer settling the employee's personal credit card bill
options: Not assessable
Assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the cost
questions.explain: Discharging the employee's own liability is assessable under the s.9(1)(a)(iv) liability test, even though no cash passes to the employee.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
A corporate club membership in the company's name, used by an employee
options: Assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Not assessable
Assessable only at 50% of the cost
questions.explain: Where the liability is the employer's and the benefit is not convertible into money, it falls outside the charge.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
Reimbursement of an employee's deductible self-education expenses
options: Assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the cost
Not assessable
questions.explain: Reimbursed self-education expenses are not taxable; correspondingly no deduction is available for the reimbursed portion. Taxing them is a reported error.

questions.q: On what value is a share award benefit assessed?
options: The market value on the date the shares vest
The market value on the date the award is granted
The price paid by the employee
The average of the grant and vesting values
questions.explain: A share award is assessed on the market value when the shares vest. Using the grant-date value is named in the June 2026 report as a common error. Contrast a share option, which is assessed on the gain at exercise, assignment or release.

questions.q: A share option has a vesting period of 730 days, of which 292 were spent working in Hong Kong. What proportion of the gain on exercise is assessable to Hong Kong salaries tax?
questions.explain: The gain is apportioned by reference to the days of the vesting period attributable to Hong Kong services: 292/730 = 40%.

questions.q: A share option has a vesting period of 1095 days, of which 365 were spent working in Hong Kong. What proportion of the gain on exercise is assessable to Hong Kong salaries tax?
questions.explain: The gain is apportioned by reference to the days of the vesting period attributable to Hong Kong services: 365/1095 = 33%.

questions.q: A share option has a vesting period of 365 days, of which 146 were spent working in Hong Kong. What proportion of the gain on exercise is assessable to Hong Kong salaries tax?
questions.explain: The gain is apportioned by reference to the days of the vesting period attributable to Hong Kong services: 146/365 = 40%.

questions.q: How is a contractual gratuity payable on completion of a fixed-term contract treated?
options: Assessable in full as income from employment
Exempt as a capital receipt
Assessable at 50%
Exempt if paid after the employment ends
questions.explain: A gratuity payable under the contract is a reward for services and is fully assessable. Contrast genuine severance and long service payments under the Employment Ordinance, which are not.

questions.q: How is a statutory severance payment under the Employment Ordinance treated?
options: Fully assessable as income from employment
Not assessable, to the extent of the statutory entitlement
Assessable at 50%
Assessable only if the employee is re-employed within 12 months
questions.explain: Statutory severance and long service payments are compensation for loss of office rather than a reward for services, and are not assessable to the extent of the statutory entitlement.

questions.q:
What is the maximum annual deduction for the following?
Self-education expenses
questions.explain: Capped at $100,000 a year. Reimbursed amounts are excluded.

questions.q:
What is the maximum annual deduction for the following?
Mandatory MPF contributions by an employee
questions.explain: Capped at $18,000 - the statutory maximum mandatory contribution.

questions.q:
What is the maximum annual deduction for the following?
Elderly residential care expenses, per parent or grandparent
questions.explain: Capped at $110,000 per dependant, and mutually exclusive with the dependent parent allowance for the same person.

questions.q:
What is the maximum annual deduction for the following?
Home loan interest, without a qualifying child
questions.explain: Capped at $100,000, for up to 20 years of assessment, and apportioned among joint owners or tenants in common by ownership share.

questions.q:
What is the maximum annual deduction for the following?
Qualifying premiums under a VHIS certified plan, per insured person
questions.explain: Capped at $8,000 per insured person, with no limit on the number of insured persons.

questions.q:
What is the maximum annual deduction for the following?
Qualifying annuity premiums and MPF voluntary contributions combined
questions.explain: A single combined cap of $60,000, with tax-deductible voluntary contributions deducted first.

questions.q:
What is the maximum annual deduction for the following?
Domestic rents for a non-owner-occupier, without a qualifying child
questions.explain: Capped at $100,000, rising to $120,000 where there is a qualifying child.

questions.q:
What is the maximum annual deduction for the following?
Assisted reproductive services expenses
questions.explain: Capped at $100,000, available from YA 2024/25.

questions.q: A taxpayer's income after other deductions is $1,514,700 and approved charitable donations of $100,000 were paid. What deduction is allowed?
questions.explain: Donations are capped at 35% of income after the other deductions: 35% × $1,514,700 = $530,145, so the allowable amount is $100,000. Any excess simply lapses - there is no carry-forward for salaries tax deductions.

questions.q: A taxpayer's income after other deductions is $490,000 and approved charitable donations of $210,000 were paid. What deduction is allowed?
questions.explain: Donations are capped at 35% of income after the other deductions: 35% × $490,000 = $171,500, so the allowable amount is $171,500. Any excess simply lapses - there is no carry-forward for salaries tax deductions.

questions.q: A taxpayer's income after other deductions is $800,000 and approved charitable donations of $350,000 were paid. What deduction is allowed?
questions.explain: Donations are capped at 35% of income after the other deductions: 35% × $800,000 = $280,000, so the allowable amount is $280,000. Any excess simply lapses - there is no carry-forward for salaries tax deductions.

questions.q: What is the statutory test for deducting an employee's outgoings and expenses?
options: Incurred to the extent of producing the assessable income
Wholly, exclusively and necessarily incurred in the production of the assessable income
Reasonably incurred in connection with the employment
Incurred for the convenience of the employer
questions.explain: Section 12(1)(a) is deliberately stricter than the profits tax test: wholly, exclusively and necessarily, not merely 'to the extent'. Very few ordinary employment expenses pass it (DIPN 9).

questions.q: How is the cost of travelling between home and the workplace treated?
options: Deductible in full
Deductible at 50%
Not deductible - it is a domestic or private expense
Deductible up to $100,000
questions.explain: Home-to-work travel is a domestic or private expense and is expressly outside s.12(1)(a). Travel between two workplaces in the course of duties is deductible.

questions.q: For the year of assessment 2025/26 - the basis examined in December 2026 - what is the basic allowance?
questions.explain: $132,000 on the exam basis. On the current YA 2026/27 basis it is $145,000. IRD publishes 2024/25 and 2025/26 as a single column, so one figure covers TX-HKG from June 2025 through December 2026.

questions.q: For the year of assessment 2025/26 - the basis examined in December 2026 - what is the married person's allowance?
questions.explain: $264,000 on the exam basis. On the current YA 2026/27 basis it is $290,000. IRD publishes 2024/25 and 2025/26 as a single column, so one figure covers TX-HKG from June 2025 through December 2026.

questions.q: For the year of assessment 2025/26 - the basis examined in December 2026 - what is the child allowance for each of the 1st to 9th child?
questions.explain: $130,000 on the exam basis. On the current YA 2026/27 basis it is $140,000. IRD publishes 2024/25 and 2025/26 as a single column, so one figure covers TX-HKG from June 2025 through December 2026.

questions.q: For the year of assessment 2025/26 - the basis examined in December 2026 - what is the dependent parent allowance for a parent aged 60 or above, not residing with the taxpayer?
questions.explain: $50,000 on the exam basis. On the current YA 2026/27 basis it is $55,000. IRD publishes 2024/25 and 2025/26 as a single column, so one figure covers TX-HKG from June 2025 through December 2026.

questions.q: For the year of assessment 2025/26 - the basis examined in December 2026 - what is the single parent allowance?
questions.explain: $132,000 on the exam basis. On the current YA 2026/27 basis it is $145,000. IRD publishes 2024/25 and 2025/26 as a single column, so one figure covers TX-HKG from June 2025 through December 2026.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the married person's allowance and the basic allowance?
options: Exactly twice the basic allowance
Two and a half times the basic allowance
One and a half times the basic allowance
The same as the basic allowance
questions.explain: The married person's allowance is exactly double the basic. This is why joint assessment gives a couple nothing on allowances where both already absorb their own - it only helps where one spouse cannot.

questions.q: A taxpayer's mother holds a Hong Kong identity card but lives permanently outside Hong Kong. Can the dependent parent allowance be claimed?
options: Yes - holding a Hong Kong identity card is sufficient
No - the parent must be ordinarily resident in Hong Kong
Yes, provided the parent is aged 60 or above
Yes, if the taxpayer contributes at least $12,000 a year
questions.explain: The parent must be ordinarily resident in Hong Kong. An identity card is evidence, not the test. The June 2026 report names claiming the allowance for such a parent as a common error.

questions.q: Two siblings each contribute to the maintenance of the same dependent parent. How is the dependent parent allowance given?
options: Each may claim half
Both may claim it in full
Only one of them may claim it, as agreed between them
Neither may claim it
questions.explain: Only one person may claim the allowance for any one dependant in a year of assessment. Where more than one is eligible they must agree; if they cannot, no one gets it.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the dependent parent allowance and the deduction for elderly residential care expenses?
options: Both may be claimed in full for the same parent
Both may be claimed but each is halved
The allowance is available only if the deduction is not claimed in full
Mutually exclusive - only one may be claimed for the same parent
questions.explain: They cannot both be claimed for the same parent in the same year. Compute both and take whichever is worth more.

questions.q: A taxpayer's net income before allowances is $1,396,700 and the allowances claimed total $145,000 (single, basic allowance only). What is the salaries tax payable, ignoring any one-off reduction?
questions.explain: Compute twice and pay the lower: progressive rates on net chargeable income of $1,251,700 give $194,789; the standard rate on net income of $1,396,700 - before allowances - gives $209,505. The lower is $194,789. Applying the standard rate to net chargeable income is the single commonest error in this computation.

questions.q: A taxpayer's net income before allowances is $266,000 and the allowances claimed total $145,000 (single, basic allowance only). What is the salaries tax payable, ignoring any one-off reduction?
questions.explain: Compute twice and pay the lower: progressive rates on net chargeable income of $121,000 give $6,100; the standard rate on net income of $266,000 - before allowances - gives $39,900. The lower is $6,100. Applying the standard rate to net chargeable income is the single commonest error in this computation.

questions.q: A taxpayer's net income before allowances is $1,049,800 and the allowances claimed total $145,000 (single, basic allowance only). What is the salaries tax payable, ignoring any one-off reduction?
questions.explain: Compute twice and pay the lower: progressive rates on net chargeable income of $904,800 give $135,816; the standard rate on net income of $1,049,800 - before allowances - gives $157,470. The lower is $135,816. Applying the standard rate to net chargeable income is the single commonest error in this computation.

questions.q: A taxpayer's net income before allowances is $600,000 and the allowances claimed total $290,000 (married, married person's allowance). What is the salaries tax payable, ignoring any one-off reduction?
questions.explain: Compute twice and pay the lower: progressive rates on net chargeable income of $310,000 give $34,700; the standard rate on net income of $600,000 - before allowances - gives $90,000. The lower is $34,700. Applying the standard rate to net chargeable income is the single commonest error in this computation.

questions.q: What is the salaries tax standard rate from the year of assessment 2024/25?
options: 15% on the first $5,000,000 of net income and 16% on the remainder
A flat 15% on net income
A flat 16% on net income
15% on net chargeable income
questions.explain: The standard rate became two-tiered from YA 2024/25: 15% on the first $5,000,000 of net income, 16% above. It applies to net income before personal allowances, and the taxpayer pays the lower of this and the progressive computation.

questions.q: What are the progressive rates applied to net chargeable income?
options: 2%, 7%, 12% and 17% on four bands of $50,000
2%, 6%, 10% and 14% on four successive bands of $50,000, then 17%
5%, 10% and 15% on three bands of $40,000, then 17%
A flat 15%
questions.explain: Four bands of $50,000 at 2%, 6%, 10% and 14%, then 17% on the remainder. Unchanged on both the current and the exam basis.

questions.q: When is an election for joint assessment under s.10(2) beneficial?
options: Whenever both spouses have income
Whenever the couple have children
Where one spouse cannot fully absorb their own allowances
Whenever one spouse pays the standard rate
questions.explain: Only where one spouse's income is too low to absorb their allowances, so the unused part shelters the other's income. Where both already absorb their own, the married person's allowance is exactly twice the basic and aggregating merely drags the lower earner's income into the higher marginal band.

questions.q: A married couple are separately assessed. Which spouse should claim their approved charitable donations?
options: The spouse who actually paid them
They must be split equally
The spouse with the lower income
The spouse with the higher marginal rate and sufficient cap
questions.explain: Donations may be claimed by either spouse regardless of who paid. Allocate them to the spouse with the higher marginal rate and enough 35% cap to absorb them. The June 2026 report notes candidates failed to advise this.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
An air ticket provided once every two years under an employment contract, for the employee to visit their home country
options: Assessable
Not assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the value
questions.explain: Home leave passage benefits are assessable in full, whether provided in kind or reimbursed, under s.9(1)(a) as a reward for services - there is no exemption for 'home leave' as such.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
A low-interest loan from the employer, where the interest actually charged is below market rate but is not waived
options: Assessable
Not assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the value
questions.explain: The interest saved on a loan is not itself convertible into money and does not discharge any liability of the employee, so - unlike a loan later waived in full or in part - it is outside the charge.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
The employer waiving repayment of an employee loan
options: Not assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable
Assessable only at 50% of the value
questions.explain: Waiving a debt discharges the employee's own liability and is assessable under the s.9(1)(a)(iv) liability test, in contrast to the interest-saved scenario above where no liability is discharged.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
A cash allowance paid to the employee to cover the cost of meals
options: Not assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the value
Assessable
questions.explain: A cash allowance, however described, is simply additional cash pay and is fully assessable - contrast free meals provided in kind at the workplace, which DIPN 41 treats as a non-assessable benefit in specified circumstances.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
Free meals provided at the employer's canteen on the business premises during working hours
options: Not assessable
Assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the value
questions.explain: DIPN 41 accepts that meals provided in kind at the workplace are not assessable, unlike a cash meal allowance which is simply pay.

questions.q:
How is the following treated for salaries tax purposes?
A cash bonus tied to the employee remaining in service until a future date, paid after that date
options: Not assessable
Assessable
Assessable only if the employee is a director
Assessable only at 50% of the value
questions.explain: A retention bonus is still a reward for services and is assessable when it accrues - normally the date the entitlement to it becomes vested, i.e. when the condition is satisfied, not the date of the underlying agreement.

questions.q: A discretionary bonus for the year ended 31 March 2026 is only decided by the board and paid in July 2026. In which year of assessment does it accrue?
options: The date the income is actually paid into the employee's bank account
The date the employment contract was originally signed
The date the employee becomes entitled to the income - normally when the services giving rise to it have been rendered
The end of the year of assessment in which the amount is finally quantified
questions.explain: Income accrues when the employee becomes entitled to it. A discretionary bonus is not accrued until the discretion is actually exercised, so it falls into the year of assessment in which the board's decision is made and the entitlement crystallises - here 2026/27, not the earlier year the bonus related to and not simply the date of payment.

questions.q: How is a gain on a share option granted to an employee normally taxed, where the option itself has no ascertainable market value at grant?
options: Assessable in the year the option is exercised, assigned or released, on the gain realised then
Never assessable, being a capital gain on shares
Assessable equally over the vesting period, year by year
Assessable in the year the option is granted, on its value at grant, with no further charge on exercise
questions.explain: Where an option cannot be valued when granted - the usual case for an employee share option - no charge arises at grant. The charge instead falls in the year the option is exercised, assigned or released, on the difference between the market value of the shares and the exercise price paid.

questions.q: What is the effect of the 'deemed exercise' rule where a share option remains unexercised for a long period?
options: The employee is treated as having elected to defer the option gain, but must include it within 3 years of the grant even if not yet exercised, assigned or released
The gain simply escapes salaries tax if the option is still unexercised after 3 years
The employee must pay tax annually on the unrealised paper gain
The 3-year rule only applies to options over shares in a listed company
questions.explain: To stop indefinite deferral, an employee share option must be brought into charge within 3 years of the date of grant even if it has not by then been exercised, assigned or released, valuing the gain as if it had been exercised at that point.

questions.q: An employee contributes to the mandatory tier of their MPF scheme. How is the deduction restricted?
options: Not deductible at all - only the employer's contributions count
Deductible up to the actual mandatory contribution, capped at $18,000, even where the employee is also a member of a recognised occupational retirement scheme
Deductible without limit
Deductible only if the employee is self-employed
questions.explain: Section 26G caps the deduction at the amount that would be required as a mandatory contribution, currently capped at $18,000 a year - voluntary top-ups beyond the mandatory amount get no deduction at all under salaries tax.

questions.q: What is the nature of the one-off salaries tax reduction the Financial Secretary has announced in several recent Budgets?
options: It is a permanent reduction in the tax rates, written into the Ordinance
It applies automatically to provisional tax but never to final tax
A person's total tax for the year is reduced by a percentage, up to a specified cap, announced separately each year in the Budget
It applies only to taxpayers earning below the basic allowance
questions.explain: It is a one-off, Budget-announced concession - a percentage reduction of the final tax payable, subject to a specified dollar cap for that year of assessment - and needs separate legislation each time; it is not a permanent feature of the Inland Revenue Ordinance and a candidate should not assume it repeats automatically without being told.

questions.q: For which taxpayer is an election for joint assessment under s.10(2) most likely to be worthwhile?
options: A married person whose spouse also earns a substantial salary and fully uses their own allowances
An unmarried taxpayer with no dependants
A taxpayer who has already elected personal assessment
A married person whose spouse has little or no income of their own
questions.explain: Joint assessment only helps where one spouse's own income cannot absorb their personal allowances - the unused portion then shelters the other spouse's income. Where both spouses already have enough income to use their own allowances, joint assessment achieves nothing and can even push income into a higher marginal band.

questions.q: A couple marry partway through the year of assessment. How is the married person's allowance affected?
options: A person is regarded as married throughout the year of assessment if married for any part of it, but the allowance is time-apportioned only in the year of marriage or divorce for certain allowances, not the married person's allowance itself
The married person's allowance is always time-apportioned by the number of months of the marriage
No allowance at all is given in the year of marriage
The full married person's allowance requires the marriage to have subsisted for the whole year
questions.explain: The married person's allowance is an all-or-nothing allowance for the whole year if the couple were married for any part of the year of assessment - it is not time-apportioned by the number of months married, unlike some other reliefs that do prorate.

questions.q: A taxpayer's child is born in November, partway through the year of assessment. How much child allowance can be claimed for that year?
options: The child allowance is apportioned by the number of months the child was alive during the year
A child born during the year still qualifies for the full child allowance for that year - it is not time-apportioned either
No child allowance is given in the year of birth
Only half the child allowance is given in the year of birth
questions.explain: Like the married person's allowance, the child allowance is not time-apportioned - the full annual amount is given for the year of birth, and again for the year the child ceases to qualify (for instance turning 18 without continuing full-time education).

questions.q: What additional, one-off allowance is available in the year a child is born, on top of the ordinary child allowance for that child?
options: Double the ordinary child allowance in the year of birth
No additional allowance is available
An additional one-ninth of the basic child allowance for that child, given only in the year of birth
An additional allowance equal to the elderly residential care cap
questions.explain: An additional child allowance is given for the year of birth - it is not an extra allowance in every year, only the birth year - to help offset the immediate costs of a new baby.

questions.q: What are the basic conditions for claiming the child allowance?
options: Only children under 12 qualify
The child must live in the same household as the taxpayer at all times
Only the taxpayer's own biological children qualify - not adopted or step-children

The taxpayer must have maintained the child, wholly or substantially at the taxpayer's own expense, and the child must be under 18, or under 25 and receiving full-time education, or incapacitated for work
questions.explain: The child must be maintained by the claimant, be unmarried, and be either under 18, or under 25 and still receiving full-time education, or incapacitated for work by physical or mental disability - and 'child' includes an adopted child, a step-child and an illegitimate child, not only a legitimate biological one.

questions.q: Who is chargeable to profits tax and on what?
options: A person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong, on profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong from that trade, profession or business
Any person resident in Hong Kong, on worldwide profits
A company incorporated in Hong Kong, on all profits wherever arising
Any person carrying on business in Hong Kong, on all profits received in Hong Kong
questions.explain: Section 14(1) charges every person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong, on profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong from that trade, profession or business. Hong Kong operates a strict territorial, source-based system - residence and place of incorporation are irrelevant, and offshore profits are outside the charge however the money is received.

questions.q: How is the source of profits determined, following HK-TVB v CIR and later cases?
options: Decided solely by where the contract of sale was signed
A question of fact, decided by looking at what the taxpayer did to earn the profit and where they did it
Decided solely by where the taxpayer is incorporated
Decided solely by where the goods are physically delivered
questions.explain: The 'operations test': look at what the taxpayer actually did to earn the profit in question, and where. It is a practical, fact-specific enquiry, not a single mechanical rule - contract location and place of incorporation are each relevant but never decisive on their own.

questions.q: For a business of trading in goods, what is the primary factor in determining the source of the trading profit?
options: Where the goods are manufactured
Where the goods are physically stored before sale
Where the contracts of purchase and sale are effected
Where the company's bank account is held
questions.explain: For trading profits the place where the contracts of purchase and sale are effected is the key factor - not necessarily where they are signed, but where the effective negotiation happens. A contract effected outside Hong Kong points to an offshore claim.

questions.q: A Hong Kong company has goods manufactured under a contract-processing arrangement in the Mainland, and sells the goods from Hong Kong. How is the profit sourced?
options: All profits are Hong Kong sourced because the company is Hong Kong incorporated
All profits are offshore because the manufacturing takes place across the border
The profit follows wherever the raw materials were bought
Manufacturing profits are apportioned between the processing and the trading/selling functions
questions.explain: DIPN 21 apportions the profit 50:50 between the Mainland processing operation and the Hong Kong trading operation, reflecting that both contribute to earning it. An import-processing arrangement, by contrast, is not apportioned in the same way because the Mainland entity's own factory does the work.

questions.q: What is the basic rule for sourcing profits from the provision of services?
options: Fees for services are sourced where the services are rendered
Fees for services are always Hong Kong sourced if invoiced from Hong Kong
Fees for services are sourced where the client is based
Fees for services are always apportioned 50:50
questions.explain: Profits from services are sourced where the services are rendered - a different test from trading profits, which look at where contracts are effected.

questions.q:
Which of the 'badges of trade' does the following describe?
A short period of ownership before resale
options: It is conclusive proof of a capital transaction
It is a badge of trade indicating a trading, not a capital, transaction
It is irrelevant to the trade/capital distinction
It only matters for property transactions
questions.explain: The badges of trade (subject matter, length of ownership, frequency, supplementary work, circumstances of realisation, motive) are drawn from case law and none is conclusive alone - the question is always the overall impression from all the facts.

questions.q:
Which of the 'badges of trade' does the following describe?
The taxpayer's stated intention at the time of acquisition, taken with the surrounding circumstances
options: It is the sole and conclusive test of trading
It is irrelevant if not stated in writing
It is one badge of trade among several, not conclusive on its own
It only applies to individuals, not companies
questions.explain: The badges of trade (subject matter, length of ownership, frequency, supplementary work, circumstances of realisation, motive) are drawn from case law and none is conclusive alone - the question is always the overall impression from all the facts.

questions.q:
Which of the 'badges of trade' does the following describe?
The number and frequency of similar transactions
options: A single transaction can never be trading
Frequency is irrelevant to the badges of trade
Only three or more transactions can amount to trading
Repeated, systematic transactions point towards trading
questions.explain: The badges of trade (subject matter, length of ownership, frequency, supplementary work, circumstances of realisation, motive) are drawn from case law and none is conclusive alone - the question is always the overall impression from all the facts.

questions.q:
Which of the 'badges of trade' does the following describe?
An asset acquired to be modified or improved before resale
options: Work done to make an asset more saleable is a badge of trade
Modification is only relevant to manufacturing businesses
Modification always indicates a capital asset
Modification is irrelevant unless done by a contractor
questions.explain: The badges of trade (subject matter, length of ownership, frequency, supplementary work, circumstances of realisation, motive) are drawn from case law and none is conclusive alone - the question is always the overall impression from all the facts.

questions.q: A company receives a lump sum as compensation for the permanent loss of an agency it held, the agency being a capital asset of the business. How is the receipt treated?
options: A trading receipt, taxable in full
A capital receipt, outside the scope of profits tax
Taxable at 50% of the sum received
Exempt only if received from a connected party
questions.explain: Compensation for the loss or sterilisation of a capital asset is itself capital, following Van den Berghs v Clark. Contrast compensation for loss of trading stock or lost profits, which is a revenue receipt.

questions.q: An insurer pays out for trading stock destroyed by fire. How is the payment treated?
options: A capital receipt, outside the charge
Taxable only when the goods are eventually resold
A revenue receipt, taxable in the year it accrues
Taxable at half the normal rate
questions.explain: Compensation that replaces a revenue item - here, stock that would have been sold in the ordinary course - is itself revenue in nature and taxable.

questions.q: What is the statutory test for deducting an expense under profits tax?
options: Outgoings and expenses wholly, exclusively and necessarily incurred in the production of assessable profits
Any expense recorded in the accounts
Outgoings incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the trade
Outgoings and expenses to the extent incurred in the production of assessable profits
questions.explain: Section 16(1) is deliberately looser than the salaries tax test: expenses to the extent incurred in the production of profits. There is no 'wholly, exclusively and necessarily' requirement, so an expense with a dual purpose can still be apportioned and partly deducted.

questions.q: Which of the following IS normally deductible under s.17?
options: Capital expenditure
Domestic or private expenditure
Expenditure not incurred in the production of profits
Rent of business premises
questions.explain: Section 17(1) specifically prohibits deducting capital expenditure, domestic or private expenditure, and expenses not incurred in the production of chargeable profits. Ordinary business rent is none of these and is deductible under s.16(1).

questions.q: A trader incurs legal costs in acquiring a new shop lease for the business. How is the expenditure treated?
options: Deductible in full as a trading expense
Not deductible - it is capital expenditure
Deductible over five years
Deductible only if the taxpayer is a company
questions.explain: Costs of acquiring a capital asset - including the legal costs of acquiring it - are themselves capital and non-deductible, even though the asset itself (the lease) will be used to earn trading profits.

questions.q: A company incurs legal costs defending a claim brought by a customer over defective goods sold in the ordinary course of business. How are the costs treated?
options: Not deductible as it relates to litigation
Deductible only up to $50,000
Deductible - it is incurred in defending the taxpayer's trading position
Not deductible as legal costs are always capital
questions.explain: Legal costs take their character from what they protect. Costs incurred in the ordinary course of trade - defending a trading claim, recovering a trading debt - are revenue and deductible. Costs of acquiring or defending title to a capital asset are not.

questions.q: A company's assessable profits before deducting donations are $500,000, and it made approved charitable donations of $30,000 in the year. What deduction is allowed?
questions.explain: Section 16D caps the deduction at 35% of assessable profits before the donation itself is deducted: 35% × $500,000 = $175,000. Here the allowable amount is $30,000. The donation must also be at least $100 and not merely a payment for goods, advertising space or a dinner ticket at an inflated price.

questions.q: A company's assessable profits before deducting donations are $280,000, and it made approved charitable donations of $15,000 in the year. What deduction is allowed?
questions.explain: Section 16D caps the deduction at 35% of assessable profits before the donation itself is deducted: 35% × $280,000 = $98,000. Here the allowable amount is $15,000. The donation must also be at least $100 and not merely a payment for goods, advertising space or a dinner ticket at an inflated price.

questions.q: A company's assessable profits before deducting donations are $900,000, and it made approved charitable donations of $60,000 in the year. What deduction is allowed?
questions.explain: Section 16D caps the deduction at 35% of assessable profits before the donation itself is deducted: 35% × $900,000 = $315,000. Here the allowable amount is $60,000. The donation must also be at least $100 and not merely a payment for goods, advertising space or a dinner ticket at an inflated price.

questions.q: A company replaces a factory's flat roof with a completely new and improved roof structure of superior design, rather than patching the original. How is the cost treated?
options: Deductible in full as a repair
Deductible at 50%, the balance capitalised
Not deductible - it is capital in nature
Deductible only if the roof was under one year old
questions.explain: A repair restores an asset; an improvement makes it better than before and is capital. Replacing with something of a materially superior specification tips this into capital expenditure, non-deductible under s.17(1)(c), though it may qualify for a depreciation allowance instead.

questions.q: A trader makes a specific provision against a named customer's debt, having reasonable grounds to believe it will not be paid. Is the provision deductible?
options: Not deductible - only debts formally written off are allowed
Deductible only for banks
Not deductible - a general provision
Deductible - a specific provision for a debt reasonably estimated to be irrecoverable
questions.explain: Section 16(1)(d) allows a deduction for bad debts and doubtful debts specifically identified as estimated to be bad. A general, unspecific provision (e.g. 2% of all debtors) is never deductible.

questions.q: A bad debt previously allowed as a deduction is unexpectedly recovered in a later year. How is the recovery treated?
options: Assessable as a trading receipt in the year recovered
Not assessable, as it was never allowed as a deduction
Related back to the year the debt was written off
Assessable at half the amount recovered
questions.explain: The recovery is a trading receipt of the year it is received, taxable in full, mirroring the property tax treatment of recovered irrecoverable rent.

questions.q: Under what condition is interest expense generally deductible against profits tax?
options: Never deductible under profits tax
Deductible - interest on money borrowed for the purposes of producing chargeable profits, subject to the anti-avoidance conditions in s.16(2)
Deductible only if paid to a Hong Kong bank
Deductible only up to the amount of profits before interest
questions.explain: Section 16(1)(a) allows interest on borrowings used to produce chargeable profits, but s.16(2) imposes several conditions aimed at related-party and circular back-to-back arrangements - interest paid to an overseas associate not itself subject to Hong Kong profits tax on the interest, for instance, can be restricted.

questions.q: What initial allowance is available on qualifying capital expenditure on plant or machinery?
options: 60% of the cost, apportioned by the number of months of use
20% of the cost, in the year of purchase
60% of the cost, in the year of purchase, regardless of how long the asset is used in the year
There is no initial allowance for plant and machinery
questions.explain: Section 39B(1A) gives a flat 60% initial allowance in the year of purchase, with no time-apportionment for part of a year and no reduction for private use by a company - private use apportionment applies to sole traders and partnerships, not companies.

questions.q: At what rates is the annual allowance on plant and machinery computed?
options: A flat 25% a year on the reducing balance
20% a year on the original cost, straight line
4% a year on the reducing balance
10%, 20% or 30% a year on the reducing balance of each pool
questions.explain: Assets are grouped into pools taxed at 10%, 20% or 30% depending on their prescribed class, each on the reducing balance of that pool's written-down value.

questions.q: A 30%-pool has a written-down value brought forward of $800,000. During the year the business bought qualifying plant for $200,000 and sold plant for $50,000. What is the total depreciation allowance for the year?
questions.explain: Additions $200,000 less the 60% initial allowance $120,000 leaves $880,000; less disposal proceeds of $50,000 = $830,000; the annual allowance is 30% of that = $249,000. Total allowance = IA $120,000 + AA $249,000 = $369,000. Deducting disposal proceeds before the initial allowance, or omitting the IA entirely, are the two errors most often made.

questions.q: A pool taxed at 20% has a written-down value brought forward of $1,500,000. During the year the business bought qualifying plant for $100,000 and sold plant for $300,000. What is the total depreciation allowance for the year?
questions.explain: Additions $100,000 less the 60% initial allowance $60,000 leaves $1,540,000; less disposal proceeds of $300,000 = $1,240,000; the annual allowance is 20% of that = $248,000. Total allowance = IA $60,000 + AA $248,000 = $308,000. Deducting disposal proceeds before the initial allowance, or omitting the IA entirely, are the two errors most often made.

questions.q: A pool taxed at 10% has a written-down value brought forward of $0. During the year the business bought qualifying plant for $600,000 and sold plant for $0. What is the total depreciation allowance for the year?
questions.explain: Additions $600,000 less the 60% initial allowance $360,000 leaves $240,000; less disposal proceeds of $0 = $240,000; the annual allowance is 10% of that = $24,000. Total allowance = IA $360,000 + AA $24,000 = $384,000. Deducting disposal proceeds before the initial allowance, or omitting the IA entirely, are the two errors most often made.

questions.q: A 30%-pool has a written-down value brought forward of $450,000. During the year the business bought qualifying plant for $150,000 and sold plant for $100,000. What is the total depreciation allowance for the year?
questions.explain: Additions $150,000 less the 60% initial allowance $90,000 leaves $510,000; less disposal proceeds of $100,000 = $410,000; the annual allowance is 30% of that = $123,000. Total allowance = IA $90,000 + AA $123,000 = $213,000. Deducting disposal proceeds before the initial allowance, or omitting the IA entirely, are the two errors most often made.

questions.q: Disposal proceeds from selling the only asset in a pool exceed its written-down value brought forward, after also deducting the year's additions. What is the tax result?
options: A balancing charge, added back to assessable profits
A balancing allowance, deducted from assessable profits
No adjustment - the excess is simply ignored
The excess is carried forward as a loss
questions.explain: Where proceeds exceed the pool's residue, the excess is a balancing charge - effectively clawing back allowances given in earlier years - and is added back as if it were extra profit, capped at the total allowances actually given. Where proceeds are less than the residue and the pool ceases to have any asset in it, the shortfall is a balancing allowance instead.

questions.q: Plant is acquired on hire purchase with a deposit of $60,000, and 6 monthly instalments are paid in the year, each with a capital element of $8,000. What initial allowance is available for the year?
questions.explain: For hire purchase, the initial allowance runs only on the capital sums actually paid in the year - the deposit plus the capital element of instalments paid - not on the full cash price of the asset: ($60,000 + 6 × $8,000) × 60% = $64,800. Using the full cash price overstates the allowance.

questions.q: Plant is acquired on hire purchase with a deposit of $100,000, and 4 monthly instalments are paid in the year, each with a capital element of $12,000. What initial allowance is available for the year?
questions.explain: For hire purchase, the initial allowance runs only on the capital sums actually paid in the year - the deposit plus the capital element of instalments paid - not on the full cash price of the asset: ($100,000 + 4 × $12,000) × 60% = $88,800. Using the full cash price overstates the allowance.

questions.q: Plant is acquired on hire purchase with a deposit of $40,000, and 9 monthly instalments are paid in the year, each with a capital element of $5,000. What initial allowance is available for the year?
questions.explain: For hire purchase, the initial allowance runs only on the capital sums actually paid in the year - the deposit plus the capital element of instalments paid - not on the full cash price of the asset: ($40,000 + 9 × $5,000) × 60% = $51,000. Using the full cash price overstates the allowance.

questions.q: What allowance is available on capital expenditure on constructing a commercial building or structure used in the business?
options: Straight-line: 20% initial allowance plus 4% annual allowance on cost
Reducing balance at 4% a year
A single 100% deduction in the year of completion
There is no allowance for commercial buildings
questions.explain: A 20% initial allowance in the year the expenditure is incurred, plus a 4% annual allowance on a straight-line basis (i.e. on cost, not written-down value) for 25 years, given to whoever owns the relevant interest at the end of the basis period. Industrial buildings attract the same rates under a parallel code.

questions.q: A company buys a completed commercial building for use in its business. On what amount is the buildings allowance computed?
options: The whole purchase price qualifies, including the land
The cost of the land itself is excluded
Only 50% of the price qualifies
The allowance is based on the rateable value
questions.explain: Only the cost of construction qualifies - the value attributable to the land must be stripped out first, whether the building was constructed by the taxpayer or bought already built.

questions.q: What allowance is available for capital expenditure on a prescribed fixed asset such as computer hardware and software, or manufacturing machinery specified by the Commissioner?
options: 60% initial allowance plus a 20% pool rate
20% initial allowance plus 4% annual allowance
100% deduction in the year of purchase
No allowance is available
questions.explain: Section 16G gives a 100% deduction in the year of purchase for prescribed fixed assets, in place of the normal pooled initial-plus-annual allowance system - though a specific exclusion applies to office furniture and fixtures, motor vehicles, and structures.

questions.q: A company incurred Type A R&D expenditure of $400,000 and Type B (qualifying) R&D expenditure of $2,500,000 in the year. What total deduction is available under s.16B?
questions.explain: Type A gets a plain 100% deduction: $400,000. Type B is enhanced - 300% on the first $2,000,000 and 200% on the excess: (min($2,500,000, 2,000,000) × 3) + (max(0, $2,500,000 - 2,000,000) × 2). Total deduction = $7,400,000. Forgetting the enhancement tiers and simply deducting 100% of the Type B spend is the commonest error - this is the exact scenario the examining team published a worked example on.

questions.q: A company incurred Type A R&D expenditure of $0 and Type B (qualifying) R&D expenditure of $3,000,000 in the year. What total deduction is available under s.16B?
questions.explain: Type A gets a plain 100% deduction: $0. Type B is enhanced - 300% on the first $2,000,000 and 200% on the excess: (min($3,000,000, 2,000,000) × 3) + (max(0, $3,000,000 - 2,000,000) × 2). Total deduction = $8,000,000. Forgetting the enhancement tiers and simply deducting 100% of the Type B spend is the commonest error - this is the exact scenario the examining team published a worked example on.

questions.q: A company incurred Type A R&D expenditure of $600,000 and Type B (qualifying) R&D expenditure of $2,400,000 in the year. What total deduction is available under s.16B?
questions.explain: Type A gets a plain 100% deduction: $600,000. Type B is enhanced - 300% on the first $2,000,000 and 200% on the excess: (min($2,400,000, 2,000,000) × 3) + (max(0, $2,400,000 - 2,000,000) × 2). Total deduction = $7,400,000. Forgetting the enhancement tiers and simply deducting 100% of the Type B spend is the commonest error - this is the exact scenario the examining team published a worked example on.

questions.q: What distinguishes 'Type B' qualifying R&D expenditure from 'Type A'?
options: Type B is any expenditure on scientific research of any kind
Type B is limited to expenditure carried out overseas
Type B must relate to one of the specified fields and either seek to extend general knowledge or have an industrial, agricultural or scientific purpose
Type B and Type A are simply two names for the same thing
questions.explain: Type B research must fall within a field specified in Schedule 45 and meet the purpose test in s.2. Type A is a residual category - R&D expenditure that does not qualify as Type B still gets a plain 100% deduction rather than none, provided it otherwise relates to the trade.

questions.q: How is an unrelieved trading loss of a Hong Kong business normally treated?
options: Carried back one year against the preceding year's profits
Lost if not used within 5 years
Set off automatically against the owner's salaries tax
Carried forward indefinitely and set off against future assessable profits of the same trade
questions.explain: Losses are carried forward with no time limit and set off against future assessable profits, but there is no carry-back and (unlike personal assessment) no automatic set-off against the owner's other income.

questions.q: A sole proprietor's business makes a loss for the year, and they also have rental income from a separate let property. How can the business loss be set against the rental income in the same year?
options: Only through electing personal assessment
Automatically, in the profits tax computation itself
By carrying it back against the previous year
It cannot be relieved against any other income
questions.explain: Only by electing personal assessment, which aggregates all the individual's chargeable income and lets a current-year business loss shelter it. Within the profits tax computation alone, the loss is simply carried forward.

questions.q: How is a partnership's trading loss for a year treated?
