options: The loss belongs to the partnership and is carried forward at partnership level only
They are shared among the partners in the profit-sharing ratio and each partner deals with their own share
The loss can only be used by the partner with the largest capital account
The loss is forfeited if any partner leaves during the year
questions.explain: The loss is allocated to the partners in the agreed profit-sharing ratio, just like a profit would be. Each partner then carries forward, or otherwise relieves, their own share - an individual partner might elect personal assessment to set it against salary; a corporate partner simply carries its share forward against future profits.

questions.q: A Hong Kong company has assessable profits of exactly $2,000,000 for the year, with no connected entities. What profits tax is payable?
options: Nil - profits below $2,000,000 are exempt
$2,000,000 × 8.25% = $165,000 - the two-tier system only changes the rate on profits above $2,000,000
It depends on an annual election by the company
questions.explain: At or below the $2,000,000 threshold the two-tier system makes no difference at all - the whole profit is simply taxed at 8.25%, the lower tier rate. The higher 16.5% rate only ever applies to the slice above $2,000,000.

questions.q: A Hong Kong company (not connected with any other entity electing the two-tier regime) has assessable profits of $2,500,000 for the year. What profits tax is payable?
questions.explain: The first $2,000,000 is taxed at 8.25%, and the excess at 16.5%: (2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($500,000 × 16.5%) = $247,500. Applying 16.5% to the whole profit, as if there were no two-tier relief, gives $412,500 and overstates the tax by $165,000.

questions.q: A Hong Kong company (not connected with any other entity electing the two-tier regime) has assessable profits of $4,200,000 for the year. What profits tax is payable?
questions.explain: The first $2,000,000 is taxed at 8.25%, and the excess at 16.5%: (2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($2,200,000 × 16.5%) = $528,000. Applying 16.5% to the whole profit, as if there were no two-tier relief, gives $693,000 and overstates the tax by $165,000.

questions.q: A Hong Kong company (not connected with any other entity electing the two-tier regime) has assessable profits of $8,000,000 for the year. What profits tax is payable?
questions.explain: The first $2,000,000 is taxed at 8.25%, and the excess at 16.5%: (2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($6,000,000 × 16.5%) = $1,155,000. Applying 16.5% to the whole profit, as if there were no two-tier relief, gives $1,320,000 and overstates the tax by $165,000.

questions.q: A Hong Kong company (not connected with any other entity electing the two-tier regime) has assessable profits of $12,000,000 for the year. What profits tax is payable?
questions.explain: The first $2,000,000 is taxed at 8.25%, and the excess at 16.5%: (2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($10,000,000 × 16.5%) = $1,815,000. Applying 16.5% to the whole profit, as if there were no two-tier relief, gives $1,980,000 and overstates the tax by $165,000.

questions.q: How does the two-tier regime apply where several companies are 'connected entities' of one another?
options: Every company in a group benefits from the two-tier rates independently
The two-tier rates are unavailable to any company in a group
The $2,000,000 threshold is doubled for a group of two companies
Only one entity in a group of connected entities may benefit from the two-tier rates; the others pay flat 16.5%/15%
questions.explain: Connected entities must nominate only one of themselves to enjoy the two-tier rates for a year of assessment; the rest pay the flat rate (16.5% corporate, 15% unincorporated) on all their profits. This stops a group multiplying the $2,000,000 band by splitting into subsidiaries.

questions.q: A sole proprietorship has assessable profits of $2,400,000. What profits tax is payable?
questions.explain: For an unincorporated business the two-tier rates are 7.5% on the first $2,000,000 and 15% above: (2,000,000 × 7.5%) + ($400,000 × 15%) = $210,000. Using the corporate rates of 8.25%/16.5% instead of 7.5%/15% is a common slip when candidates confuse the two sets of rates.

questions.q: A sole proprietorship has assessable profits of $3,600,000. What profits tax is payable?
questions.explain: For an unincorporated business the two-tier rates are 7.5% on the first $2,000,000 and 15% above: (2,000,000 × 7.5%) + ($1,600,000 × 15%) = $390,000. Using the corporate rates of 8.25%/16.5% instead of 7.5%/15% is a common slip when candidates confuse the two sets of rates.

questions.q: A sole proprietorship has assessable profits of $5,000,000. What profits tax is payable?
questions.explain: For an unincorporated business the two-tier rates are 7.5% on the first $2,000,000 and 15% above: (2,000,000 × 7.5%) + ($3,000,000 × 15%) = $600,000. Using the corporate rates of 8.25%/16.5% instead of 7.5%/15% is a common slip when candidates confuse the two sets of rates.

questions.q: How is a sole proprietor's business profit assessed to profits tax?
options: Together with the owner's salary, in one profits tax computation
At the two-tier corporate rates
Only if the business has a separate business registration number from the owner's HKID
As if the business and the owner's personal affairs were entirely separate - only business income is assessed to profits tax
questions.explain: The business is assessed on its own trading results at the unincorporated two-tier rates (7.5%/15%), entirely separately from any salaries tax on the owner's employment income - the two are only brought together if the owner elects personal assessment.

questions.q: A sole trader draws a monthly 'salary' from the business and records it as an expense. How is this treated in the profits tax computation?
options: Drawings and a notional salary to the proprietor are not deductible - the whole profit, before any such appropriation, is assessable
A reasonable salary to the proprietor is deductible, like an employee's salary
Drawings are deductible but a notional salary is not
Both are deductible provided they are recorded in the accounts
questions.explain: A proprietor cannot be their own employee. Any salary, bonus or drawings taken by a sole proprietor (or by their spouse, under s.16(2)(e)) must be added back - the entire profit before that appropriation is what is assessable.

questions.q: A sole trader pays a salary to their spouse, who works full-time managing the shop. Is the salary deductible?
options: Always deductible in full
Deductible, if the spouse genuinely works in the business and the amount is not excessive - subject to the same restriction as the proprietor's own salary
Never deductible under any circumstance
Deductible only if the spouse holds a separate business registration
questions.explain: Section 17(2) treats salaries paid to the proprietor's spouse the same way as a payment to the proprietor - it is not deductible and must be added back, regardless of how genuinely the spouse works, because husband and wife are not treated as being at arm's length for this purpose.

questions.q: How is a Hong Kong partnership assessed to profits tax?
options: The partnership is assessed and pays the tax as a single entity, like a company
Each partner is separately assessed with no reference to the partnership at all
The partnership itself is not a separate chargeable person - it files one profits tax return, but the assessable profit is allocated to and assessed on each partner individually
Only the precedent partner is assessed, on behalf of everyone
questions.explain: A partnership is not itself a person chargeable to tax, but it files one return covering the whole business (s.22), and the resulting assessable profit or loss is then divided among the partners according to their profit-sharing ratio, each partner being assessed on their own share.

questions.q: Partners are paid a salary and interest on capital under the partnership agreement, both charged as expenses in the partnership accounts. How are these treated for profits tax?
options: Deductible in the partnership computation, like a normal salary expense
Deductible for a partner who is a company, but not for an individual partner
Deductible provided the partnership agreement specifies the amount
Added back in the partnership computation, then reallocated to each partner as part of their share of profit
questions.explain: Section 16(2)(e)/(2A) treats any salary, interest on capital, or interest on loans from a partner as a mere appropriation of profit, not a real expense - it is added back in arriving at the partnership's total assessable profit, and then each partner's own salary/interest is added to their share when the profit is divided, so nothing is actually lost.

questions.q: A partnership with 3 partners has assessable profits of $3,000,000 for the year, shared 50% : 30% : 20%. One partner is a company and the rest are individuals. What is the total profits tax payable, applying the two-tier rates separately to each partner's share?
questions.explain: The $2,000,000 first-tier band is apportioned between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio, and each partner's slice of profit is then taxed at their own rates (7.5%/15% for an individual partner, 8.25%/16.5% for a corporate partner): total tax = $306,000. Applying one flat set of rates to the whole partnership profit, as if it had a single $2,000,000 band, ignores that a mixed partnership has more than one type of partner and is the error most often seen in this question.

questions.q: A partnership with 2 partners has assessable profits of $5,000,000 for the year, shared 60% : 40%. One partner is a company and the rest are individuals. What is the total profits tax payable, applying the two-tier rates separately to each partner's share?
questions.explain: The $2,000,000 first-tier band is apportioned between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio, and each partner's slice of profit is then taxed at their own rates (7.5%/15% for an individual partner, 8.25%/16.5% for a corporate partner): total tax = $624,000. Applying one flat set of rates to the whole partnership profit, as if it had a single $2,000,000 band, ignores that a mixed partnership has more than one type of partner and is the error most often seen in this question.

questions.q: A partnership with 3 partners has assessable profits of $4,000,000 for the year, shared 30% : 30% : 40%. One partner is a company and the rest are individuals. What is the total profits tax payable, applying the two-tier rates separately to each partner's share?
questions.explain: The $2,000,000 first-tier band is apportioned between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio, and each partner's slice of profit is then taxed at their own rates (7.5%/15% for an individual partner, 8.25%/16.5% for a corporate partner): total tax = $468,000. Applying one flat set of rates to the whole partnership profit, as if it had a single $2,000,000 band, ignores that a mixed partnership has more than one type of partner and is the error most often seen in this question.

questions.q: A partnership has one individual partner and one corporate partner. How does each partner's share of the partnership profit interact with personal assessment?
options: Both partners' shares are included in personal assessment
Neither partner's share can be included in personal assessment
Only the precedent partner's share is included in personal assessment
The individual partner's share is included in their personal assessment total income; the corporate partner's share never is
questions.explain: Personal assessment is available only to individuals. The individual partner's share of assessable profit (or loss) is aggregated into their own personal assessment total income, alongside salary and property income; the corporate partner's share simply stays in the corporate profits tax computation and is assessed at corporate rates with no personal assessment route available to it.

questions.q: An individual partner elects personal assessment. How is interest paid by them personally to fund their share of the partnership's borrowings restricted?
options: Restricted to that partner's own share of the partnership's net assessable value or profit, mirroring the individual property/business rule
Unlimited, the same as for a sole proprietor
Always disallowed for a partner
Capped at $100,000 regardless of the share of profit
questions.explain: The same restriction that applies to a sole proprietor's or property owner's interest applies partner by partner: it cannot exceed that partner's own share of the relevant assessable profit or net assessable value, and cannot create or increase a loss.

questions.q: At what rates is an ordinary Hong Kong company (not a qualifying professional reinsurer, corporate treasury centre or similar concessionary case) taxed on its assessable profits?
options: Whichever of the corporate or unincorporated rates gives the lower tax
Only the two-tier corporate rates of 8.25%/16.5% - the unincorporated rates never apply to a company
The unincorporated rates of 7.5%/15%
A flat rate chosen by election each year
questions.explain: A company is always taxed at the corporate two-tier rates - 8.25% on the first $2,000,000 and 16.5% above - never at the unincorporated rates, which are reserved for sole proprietorships and partnerships (other than any corporate partner within one, who is still taxed at the corporate rates on their own share).

questions.q: How does a company's payment of remuneration to its director, who is also its sole shareholder, differ in tax treatment from a sole trader's own drawings?
options: A director's remuneration must be added back, exactly as a sole proprietor's drawings are
A director's remuneration is deductible only up to 50% of profits
A director's remuneration is a deductible expense of the company - the director/shareholder is separately assessed to salaries tax on it
A director's remuneration is deductible only if the director owns no shares
questions.explain: A company is a separate legal person from its shareholders, so a director can validly be an employee of their own company: the remuneration is a normal deductible expense in the profits tax computation (subject to being reasonable in amount) and is separately taxed on the director as salaries tax. A sole proprietor has no such separate legal identity, so their own drawings are never deductible.

questions.q: How are dividends paid by a Hong Kong company treated for profits tax purposes?
options: Dividends are deductible to the company but taxable to the shareholder
Dividends are taxed twice: once to the company as a disallowed expense, and again to the shareholder
Dividends are exempt only if paid to a corporate shareholder
Dividends paid by a Hong Kong company are not deductible in computing its own profits, and are not further taxed in the hands of the shareholder
questions.explain: Dividends are a distribution of after-tax profit, not an expense, so they are never deductible to the paying company - and Hong Kong does not tax dividend income at all, so the recipient (individual or corporate) is not taxed on them either. There is no dividend withholding tax and no need for any relief against double taxation of the same profit.

questions.q: On what basis is trading stock normally valued at the end of an accounting period, for both accounting and tax purposes?
options: The lower of cost and net realisable value
Net realisable value
Original cost, regardless of any fall in value
Replacement cost
questions.explain: The lower of cost and net realisable value - a conservative basis that recognises a fall in value before the stock is sold, but never revalues stock upward above cost.

questions.q: Which cost formulas are acceptable for valuing trading stock under Hong Kong tax and accounting practice?
options: LIFO (last in, first out)
FIFO or a weighted average cost formula
The most recent purchase price applied to all units
A base stock method
questions.explain: FIFO and weighted average are both accepted. LIFO is not permitted under HKAS 2 and is not accepted for Hong Kong tax purposes either.

questions.q: A trader takes stock out of the business for personal use, or gives it away, without any question of trade to trade sale. How is this treated for profits tax?
options: At its original cost, with no profit recognised
It has no tax consequence at all
At its open market value on the date of the gift or appropriation
At half its market value
questions.explain: Section 15C deems trading stock disposed of otherwise than in the ordinary course of business - including a gift or appropriation for personal use - to be sold at open market value on that date, bringing the notional profit into the computation.

questions.q: For an established business preparing annual accounts, what is the basis period for a year of assessment?
options: The calendar year always
The year of assessment itself, from 1 April to 31 March
Whatever twelve months the taxpayer chooses each year
The accounting year ending within that year of assessment
questions.explain: The basis period is normally the accounting year ending within the year of assessment - a company with a 31 December year end is assessed for YA 2025/26 on the year ended 31 December 2025, not on the year of assessment itself.

questions.q: A business commences on 1 October 2025 and its first accounts are made up to 31 December 2026, a period of 15 months. What is the effect on the basis periods for the first two years of assessment?
options: The whole period from commencement to the end of its first accounting period may be taxed twice, in the first two years of assessment, unless the taxpayer applies for relief
The overlapping profit is automatically excluded
No overlap can ever arise under Hong Kong's basis period rules
The overlap is always resolved by extending the first accounting period to exactly 12 months
questions.explain: Because the first accounts straddle more than one year of assessment, part of the profit is included in the basis period for both YA 2025/26 (the whole first period, being the only accounts available) and YA 2026/27 (the 12 months to 31 December 2026) - the overlapping months are taxed twice unless the taxpayer successfully applies under s.18E for the assessments to be revised on a fair and just apportionment.

questions.q: A business permanently ceases on 30 June 2026, having last made up accounts to 31 December 2025. What is the basis period for the year of assessment in which it ceases?
options: The basis period is always a full 12 months
The basis period runs from the end of the previous basis period to the date of cessation
No assessment is raised for the year of cessation
The basis period is the same 12 months as the year before
questions.explain: On cessation the basis period is simply whatever period is left: from the end of the last basis period to the actual date of cessation, however short or long that turns out to be - here, 1 January to 30 June 2026.

questions.topic: Basis period - change of accounting date
questions.q: What must a business do if it wants to change its accounting year end?
options: It may change its accounting date freely with no notification needed
A change of accounting date is not permitted once a business has commenced
It must apply to the Commissioner, who may accept the change and issue directions on how the transitional basis periods are computed
It must revert to the original date within two years
questions.explain: Section 18C(3) requires the Commissioner to be satisfied of the change and to give directions on the resulting basis periods, to ensure no period of profit is missed and none is taxed twice as a result of the change.

questions.q: A company's final assessable profits for the preceding year were $2,400,000, on which the two-tier rates were applied. In the absence of any estimate supplied by the company, on what figure will provisional profits tax for the current year normally be raised?
questions.explain: Provisional profits tax is normally based on the preceding year's assessable profits, taxed at the current year's rates: $231,000, applying the two-tier rates exactly as they would to a final assessment. The company may instead apply to have it based on a lower estimate of the current year's actual profits, and must do so in writing before the return is due if it wants that lower figure used.

questions.q: A company's final assessable profits for the preceding year were $3,200,000, on which the two-tier rates were applied. In the absence of any estimate supplied by the company, on what figure will provisional profits tax for the current year normally be raised?
questions.explain: Provisional profits tax is normally based on the preceding year's assessable profits, taxed at the current year's rates: $363,000, applying the two-tier rates exactly as they would to a final assessment. The company may instead apply to have it based on a lower estimate of the current year's actual profits, and must do so in writing before the return is due if it wants that lower figure used.

questions.q: A company's final assessable profits for the preceding year were $6,000,000, on which the two-tier rates were applied. In the absence of any estimate supplied by the company, on what figure will provisional profits tax for the current year normally be raised?
questions.explain: Provisional profits tax is normally based on the preceding year's assessable profits, taxed at the current year's rates: $825,000, applying the two-tier rates exactly as they would to a final assessment. The company may instead apply to have it based on a lower estimate of the current year's actual profits, and must do so in writing before the return is due if it wants that lower figure used.

questions.q: A company's actual assessable profits turn out to be much lower than the figure on which provisional profits tax was charged. How is the provisional tax reconciled once the final assessment is made?
options: Provisional tax is always automatically refunded in full
The company forfeits the right to object to the final assessment
A note is served requiring immediate application within a set time; if refused, the excess already paid is refunded once the actual assessment is made
No adjustment is possible until the following year
questions.explain: Provisional tax already paid is set off against the final tax liability for that year, and any excess is refunded (or set against the following year's provisional tax). Before the final figures are known, the company can also apply under s.63E to hold over part of the provisional tax on prescribed grounds, such as profits being likely to be substantially lower.

questions.q: Can a loss-making Hong Kong subsidiary surrender its trading loss to a profitable fellow group company, to reduce the group's overall tax?
options: Yes - losses can be surrendered between group companies with at least 75% common ownership
Yes, but only between a parent and its wholly-owned subsidiary
Yes, automatically, with no election needed
No - each company in a group is separately assessed and a loss in one company cannot be set against profits of another
questions.explain: Hong Kong has no group loss relief at all. Each company is a separate person chargeable to profits tax in its own right; a loss simply carries forward within the loss-making company itself, however profitable the rest of the group may be. This is a frequently tested contrast with jurisdictions that do have group relief.

questions.q: What is the profits tax consequence of one group company charging another a management fee?
options: Nil - inter-company management fees, royalties and interest are all assessed and deducted on normal profits tax principles, company by company
The group is assessed as if it were one single taxpayer
Inter-company charges are always disregarded for tax purposes
Only the ultimate holding company is assessed
questions.explain: There being no group relief or consolidated filing, each company remains separately assessed: the fee is ordinary assessable income to the recipient and an ordinary deductible expense to the payer (subject to the general deduction rules), exactly as if the companies were unconnected.

questions.q: Where a taxpayer claims that profits included in its Hong Kong accounts are in fact offshore and not chargeable, where does the burden of proof lie?
options: The burden is on the Commissioner to prove the profit was derived from Hong Kong
The burden is on the taxpayer to prove the profit was not derived from Hong Kong
Profits are presumed offshore unless the Commissioner proves otherwise
There is no burden of proof - the Board of Review decides on the balance of convenience
questions.explain: Section 68(4) places the burden squarely on the taxpayer to satisfy the Commissioner (and, on appeal, the Board of Review) that the assessment is excessive or wrong - which in an offshore claim means proving what operations actually generated the profit and where they took place.

questions.q: What kind of evidence does the Inland Revenue Department expect to support an offshore profits claim?
options: A signed statement from the company's auditors
The mere fact that the customer is based outside Hong Kong
Contemporaneous documentary evidence of what was actually done and where - correspondence, contracts, travel records, minutes
The mere fact that the company has no staff physically in Hong Kong
questions.explain: IRD wants to see the operations that actually earned the profit - where negotiations happened, who visited whom, where contracts were concluded - not bare assertions. A customer's location and the absence of local staff are each a factor but neither is decisive on its own; DIPN 21 stresses that the totality of the facts is what matters.

questions.q: How is a foreign exchange gain or loss on a trade debtor denominated in a foreign currency treated for profits tax?
options: Always a capital item, outside the scope of profits tax
Always assessable in full regardless of what it relates to
Ignored entirely because Hong Kong dollar is the functional currency
A revenue receipt or loss, if it arises on a revenue account (e.g. trade debtors or creditors in foreign currency)
questions.explain: An exchange difference takes the character of the underlying item: a difference on a revenue item (trading debtors, trading creditors, floating loan capital used as working capital) is itself revenue and is taxable or deductible; a difference on a capital item (a fixed loan for acquiring a capital asset) is capital and outside the charge.

questions.q: A company borrows in US dollars to fund the purchase of a new factory building. An exchange loss arises when the loan is partly repaid. How is the loss treated?
options: Capital - the borrowing itself is a fixed capital loan used to acquire a capital asset
Revenue - all foreign currency loans are revenue in nature
It depends only on the lender's location
It is always split 50:50 between capital and revenue
questions.explain: Because the loan itself is fixed capital raised to buy a capital asset, an exchange difference on repaying it is capital and non-deductible, unlike a difference on a revenue-account trade debt.

questions.q: A company incurs marketing and staff recruitment costs while setting up a new business, several months before it actually starts trading. Are these costs deductible against the profits once trading begins?
options: Deductible in full in the first year of trading
Not deductible, because the trade had not yet commenced when the expenditure was incurred
Deductible, spread over the first three years of trading
Deductible if incurred within six months before commencement
questions.explain: Section 16(1) only allows a deduction for expenses incurred in the production of chargeable profits - which requires the trade to already exist. Genuine pre-trading expenditure is outside the charge altogether and is never deductible, however necessary it was to get the business started.

questions.q: A business pays a trade debt it still owed after it permanently ceased trading. Can this expense still be deducted?
options: Never deductible once the trade has ceased
Deductible only if paid within one month of cessation
Still deductible, provided they relate to debts or liabilities of the trade that was carried on
Deductible only against the final year's profit, never creating a loss
questions.explain: An expense does not lose its deductible character merely because the trade has since ceased, provided it genuinely relates to a liability of that trade - it is deducted in computing the profit or loss of the final basis period.

questions.q: A private investment holding company buys a block of shares intending to hold them long term for dividend income, and sells them years later at a large profit after an unsolicited takeover offer. How is the gain treated?
options: A trading transaction, taxable on the whole gain
Taxable at 50% of the gain as a compromise
Taxable only if the shares were held for less than a year
A capital asset realised without any further trading intention - the gain is not taxable
questions.explain: Realising a genuine long-term investment - even profitably, and even where the sale was prompted by someone else's offer rather than the taxpayer's own initiative - remains a capital transaction. The stated investment intention, the long holding period, and the absence of any dealing pattern all point away from trading.

questions.q: A property developer, in a transaction unrelated to its normal projects, buys a plot of land, obtains planning permission to increase its value, and resells it within the year at a profit, having taken out short-term finance for the purchase. How is the profit treated?
options: A trading transaction - an isolated adventure in the nature of trade, taxable on the whole profit
Always capital, because it was a one-off transaction
Exempt, because the taxpayer's main business is unrelated
Taxable only on 50% of the profit, as a one-off
questions.explain: Even a single, isolated transaction can amount to trading - an 'adventure in the nature of trade' - where the badges point that way: short ownership, supplementary work to enhance saleability (the planning permission), and short-term finance consistent with an intention to resell rather than hold.

questions.q: A foreign company, with no other presence in Hong Kong, licenses a patent to a Hong Kong manufacturer for use in Hong Kong and receives royalties for it. How is the royalty income treated?
options: Exempt, because the recipient has no permanent establishment in Hong Kong
Deemed to be a trading receipt of a trade carried on in Hong Kong, even though the recipient carries on no other business here
Taxable only if the recipient is a Hong Kong resident
Taxable at half the standard rate as a concession
questions.explain: Section 15(1) deems specified sums - royalties for the use of intellectual property in Hong Kong being one - to be a trading receipt arising in Hong Kong, so as to bring a non-resident owner into charge even without any physical presence here. Special reduced deemed-profit percentages then apply under s.21A depending on whether the payer is an associate.

questions.q: Under s.21A, what proportion of a royalty paid to a non-resident (who is not an associate of the payer) for the use of intellectual property in Hong Kong is deemed to be the assessable profit?
options: 100% of the gross royalty
The royalty is entirely exempt
30% of the gross royalty, taxed at the standard corporate rate - an effective rate of about 4.95% - or the full amount where paid to an associate that has claimed a Hong Kong deduction for it
50% of the gross royalty in every case
questions.explain: Only 30% of the gross sum is deemed assessable, taxed at the ordinary corporate rate, giving an effective rate of roughly 4.95% on the gross royalty. Where the recipient is an associate of the Hong Kong payer and the IP was previously owned by a person carrying on business in Hong Kong, the full 100% can instead be deemed assessable, closing off a straightforward profit-extraction route.

questions.q: A non-resident person carries on a trade in Hong Kong through a local agent, and profits arise here. How does IRD collect the tax if the non-resident itself has no assets or presence in Hong Kong?
options: No one can be assessed if the non-resident itself is untraceable
Only the non-resident's bank can be assessed
The Hong Kong customer who received the goods is automatically personally liable
The non-resident's agent, manager or representative in Hong Kong may be assessed and required to pay the tax on the non-resident's behalf
questions.explain: Section 20B lets the Commissioner assess and collect the tax from the non-resident's agent, manager, or anyone else who transacts business with or on behalf of them in Hong Kong, in the name of the non-resident.

questions.q: A Hong Kong resident's profits, already taxed in a country with which Hong Kong has no comprehensive double taxation agreement, are also taxed in Hong Kong because they are (unusually) treated as Hong Kong sourced. What relief is available under s.50?
options: Unilateral tax credit relief for the foreign tax paid, capped at the Hong Kong tax attributable to that income
No relief of any kind is available
A full deduction of the foreign tax as an expense, with no cap
Automatic exemption of the foreign-sourced income
questions.explain: Unilateral tax credit relief allows the foreign tax paid to be credited against the Hong Kong tax on the same income, but the credit can never exceed the Hong Kong tax that would otherwise be payable on that income - it cannot be used to shelter unrelated Hong Kong profits.

questions.q: What is the practical effect of Hong Kong's comprehensive double taxation agreements on profits that are genuinely offshore under Hong Kong's own source rules?
options: It brings all foreign profits into the Hong Kong charge
It has no effect - profits genuinely sourced outside Hong Kong are outside the charge regardless of any treaty
It exempts all Hong Kong profits of the resident
It replaces the territorial source test entirely
questions.explain: Hong Kong's territorial system already excludes genuinely offshore profits without needing a treaty. The DTA network mainly matters where profits would otherwise be taxed in both jurisdictions under each one's own rules, or to reduce foreign withholding tax on Hong Kong residents' cross-border income - it does not change what counts as Hong Kong-sourced in the first place.

questions.q: A Hong Kong company deposits its surplus cash with a licensed Hong Kong bank and earns interest. Is the interest chargeable to profits tax?
options: Exempt in every case, regardless of who earns it
Taxable only for individuals, never for companies
Taxable - the exemption for interest on a deposit was withdrawn for any person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong
Taxable only if the deposit is with an overseas bank
questions.explain: Since April 1998 the blanket exemption for Hong Kong-source deposit interest was withdrawn for any person carrying on business in Hong Kong: the interest is a trading receipt of the business and taxable, and, if the money deposited represents funds of the trade, it may even be considered sourced in Hong Kong on ordinary principles regardless of the deposit exemption question.

questions.q: A company insures its trading stock and premises against fire. Are the premiums deductible?
options: Never deductible - all insurance is treated as capital
Deductible only for buildings, not for plant or stock
Deductible only up to 10% of assessable profits
Deductible - insurance premiums covering the trade's own risks are a normal revenue expense
questions.explain: Ordinary business insurance premiums, covering the risks of the trade itself, are incurred in the production of profits and deductible under s.16(1) like any other overhead.

questions.q: A company is fined for breaching pollution control regulations while operating its factory. Is the fine deductible against its profits?
options: Not deductible - a fine or penalty for breaking the law is never an allowable expense, however closely connected with the trade
Deductible in full, since it arose directly from carrying on the trade
Deductible at 50%, split between the offence and the trade
Deductible only if the taxpayer successfully appeals the fine
questions.explain: A fine or penalty imposed for breaking the law is against public policy to allow as a deduction, and case law is consistent that it is never deductible, regardless of how directly it arose out of the trade.

questions.q: A company contributes to a retirement scheme for the benefit of its staff. What is the deduction limit for an ordinary (non-mandatory) employer contribution?
options: Deductible without limit
Deductible - a contribution to a recognised occupational retirement scheme or MPF scheme for employees, up to 15% of the employee's total emoluments for the year
Not deductible - only the employee's own contribution is allowed
Deductible only for a scheme registered outside Hong Kong
questions.explain: Section 16A caps the deduction for an employer's ordinary annual contribution at 15% of the total emoluments of the employees concerned for the period - a special, more generous rule applies to the special contribution made when a scheme is first set up.

questions.q: A 20%-pool has a written-down value brought forward of $300,000. During the year the business bought qualifying plant for $400,000 and sold plant for $0. What is the total depreciation allowance for the year?
questions.explain: Additions $400,000 less the 60% initial allowance $240,000 leaves a reduced pool of $460,000; the 20% annual allowance on that gives $92,000. Total allowance = IA $240,000 + AA $92,000 = $332,000.

questions.q: A 20%-pool has a written-down value brought forward of $900,000. During the year the business bought qualifying plant for $150,000 and sold plant for $200,000. What is the total depreciation allowance for the year?
questions.explain: Additions $150,000 less the 60% initial allowance $90,000 leaves a reduced pool of $760,000; the 20% annual allowance on that gives $152,000. Total allowance = IA $90,000 + AA $152,000 = $242,000.

questions.q: Who determines which of the 10%, 20% or 30% pool an item of plant or machinery falls into?
options: A trader has no general right to choose the pool rate for an asset - the rate is prescribed by the Board of Inland Revenue according to the asset's type
The trader may elect any of the three rates for any asset
All assets are pooled together at a single blended rate
The rate depends on how the taxpayer classifies the asset in its own accounts
questions.explain: The rate for each type of asset is prescribed in the Inland Revenue Rules; a taxpayer cannot simply choose a more favourable rate for an asset that does not qualify for it.

questions.q: A company takes out fidelity guarantee insurance against loss caused by employee dishonesty. Is the premium deductible?
options: It is never deductible, being akin to a private expense
It is deductible - premiums for insuring against the risk of an employee's negligence or dishonesty causing loss to the trade are a normal business expense
It is deductible only if the employee is a director
It is deductible only up to the amount of the excess/deductible under the policy
questions.explain: This protects the trade's own assets against a trading risk and is treated the same way as fire or other business insurance - a normal deductible overhead.

questions.q: On what basis is property tax charged?
options: 15% of the assessable value
16.5% of the net assessable value
15% of the net assessable value
20% of the rent received
questions.explain: Property tax is charged at the standard rate of 15% on the net assessable value of land or buildings in Hong Kong, on the owner.

questions.q: What is the assessable value of a property?
options: The open market rental value of the property
The rateable value assessed by the Rating and Valuation Department
Rent actually received in cash during the year
Consideration payable to or for the benefit of the owner for the right to use the property
questions.explain: Section 5B(2) assesses the consideration payable, in money or money's worth, for the right of use - not the market rent, not the rateable value, and on an accruals rather than a receipts basis.

questions.q: A property was let for the whole year at $25,000 a month. The owner paid rates of $9,000. The tenant paid management fees direct to the building manager. What is the property tax payable?
questions.explain: Assessable value $300,000; less rates paid by the owner $9,000 = $291,000; less the 20% statutory allowance $58,200 = net assessable value $232,800; × 15% = $34,920. Management fees paid by the tenant to a third party never enter the computation at all.

questions.q: A property was let for the whole year at $40,000 a month. The owner paid rates of $16,000. The tenant paid management fees direct to the building manager. What is the property tax payable?
questions.explain: Assessable value $480,000; less rates paid by the owner $16,000 = $464,000; less the 20% statutory allowance $92,800 = net assessable value $371,200; × 15% = $55,680. Management fees paid by the tenant to a third party never enter the computation at all.

questions.q: A property was let for the whole year at $18,000 a month. The owner paid rates of $6,500. The tenant paid management fees direct to the building manager. What is the property tax payable?
questions.explain: Assessable value $216,000; less rates paid by the owner $6,500 = $209,500; less the 20% statutory allowance $41,900 = net assessable value $167,600; × 15% = $25,140. Management fees paid by the tenant to a third party never enter the computation at all.

questions.q: A property was let for the whole year at $60,000 a month. The owner paid rates of $24,000. The tenant paid management fees direct to the building manager. What is the property tax payable?
questions.explain: Assessable value $720,000; less rates paid by the owner $24,000 = $696,000; less the 20% statutory allowance $139,200 = net assessable value $556,800; × 15% = $83,520. Management fees paid by the tenant to a third party never enter the computation at all.

questions.q: A premium of $240,000 is received on the grant of a lease for 48 months. How much is included in the assessable value for a full year?
options: Nil - a premium is a capital receipt
questions.explain: A premium is spread over the lease term but capped at 36 months: $240,000 over 36 months = $80,000 a year. Spreading over the full 48 months gives $60,000 and is wrong wherever the term exceeds three years.

questions.q: A premium of $300,000 is received on the grant of a lease for 60 months. How much is included in the assessable value for a full year?
options: Nil - a premium is a capital receipt
questions.explain: A premium is spread over the lease term but capped at 36 months: $300,000 over 36 months = $100,000 a year. Spreading over the full 60 months gives $60,000 and is wrong wherever the term exceeds three years.

questions.q: A premium of $210,000 is received on the grant of a lease for 42 months. How much is included in the assessable value for a full year?
options: Nil - a premium is a capital receipt
questions.explain: A premium is spread over the lease term but capped at 36 months: $210,000 over 36 months = $70,000 a year. Spreading over the full 42 months gives $60,000 and is wrong wherever the term exceeds three years.

questions.q: A premium of $480,000 is received on the grant of a lease for 72 months. How much is included in the assessable value for a full year?
options: Nil - a premium is a capital receipt
questions.explain: A premium is spread over the lease term but capped at 36 months: $480,000 over 36 months = $160,000 a year. Spreading over the full 72 months gives $80,000 and is wrong wherever the term exceeds three years.

questions.q: A premium of $120,000 is received on the grant of a lease for 24 months. How much is included in the assessable value for a full year?
options: $60,000 - the same figure either way
$120,000 - the premium is taxed in the year of receipt
$40,000 - spread over 36 months regardless of the term
Nil - a premium for a lease of under three years is exempt
questions.explain: The spread is over the lease term or 36 months, whichever is shorter. At 24 months the term is shorter, so $120,000 ÷ 24 × 12 = $60,000. The 36-month cap only bites on leases longer than three years.

questions.q: In which year of assessment is irrecoverable rent deducted?
options: In the year the rent accrued
In the year the rent is proved to be irrecoverable
Spread over the remaining term of the lease
Only when the tenant is formally declared bankrupt
questions.explain: Section 7C(1) gives the deduction in the year the rent is recognised as irrecoverable, not the year it accrued.

questions.q: Rent previously deducted as irrecoverable is later recovered. How is it treated?
options: Related back to the year in which it was written off
Not assessable, having already been taxed
Assessable in the year of recovery
Assessable at 50% in the year of recovery
questions.explain: It is treated as assessable value in the year of recovery. It is not related back to the year of the original deduction.

questions.q: A tenant defaults and the owner forfeits and retains the rental deposit. How is the forfeited deposit treated?
options: It is exempt as a capital receipt
It is assessable in full in addition to the irrecoverable rent deduction
It reduces the 20% statutory allowance
It is set off against the irrecoverable rent
questions.explain: The forfeited deposit is set off against the irrecoverable rent, reducing the deduction. Note the contrast: a deposit merely taken at the start of a lease is not assessable income at all - it is security held for the tenant. The June 2026 report names both errors.

questions.q: How is the statutory allowance for repairs and outgoings computed?
options: 20% of the assessable value after deducting rates paid by the owner
20% of the assessable value before deducting rates
20% of the rent actually received
The actual cost of repairs, up to 20%
questions.explain: It is a fixed 20% of the assessable value after the owner's rates. Taking it before rates, or deducting irrecoverable rent after it, both corrupt the figure.

questions.q:
In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
Government rent paid by the owner
options: Deductible
Not deductible
Deductible at 50%
Deductible only if supported by receipts
questions.explain: Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

questions.q:
In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
Mortgage interest paid by the owner
options: Deductible
Deductible at 50%
Not deductible
Deductible only if supported by receipts
questions.explain: Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

questions.q:
In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
The actual cost of repairing the roof
options: Deductible
Deductible at 50%
Deductible only if supported by receipts
Not deductible
questions.explain: Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

questions.q:
In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
The cost of replacing air-conditioners
options: Not deductible
Deductible
Deductible at 50%
Deductible only if supported by receipts
questions.explain: Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

questions.q:
In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
Rates paid by the owner
options: Not deductible
Deductible
Deductible at 50%
Deductible only if supported by receipts
questions.explain: Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

questions.q:
In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
Rates paid by the tenant direct to the Government
options: Deductible
Deductible at 50%
Not deductible
Deductible only if supported by receipts
questions.explain: Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

questions.q: What depreciation allowance is available for plant installed in a property let by an individual and charged to property tax?
options: An annual allowance of 4% of cost
An initial allowance of 20% plus 4% annually
A 100% deduction as a prescribed fixed asset
No depreciation allowance is available under property tax
questions.explain: None. Part 6 does not apply to the property tax charge - the 20% statutory allowance is the only relief. If the owner is a company carrying on business the income falls within profits tax instead, where allowances are available.

questions.q: A taxpayer owns three let properties. How is property tax computed?
options: Separately, property by property
On the aggregate of all properties owned
Separately, unless the properties are in the same building
On the aggregate, with a single 20% allowance
questions.explain: Property by property: each gets its own assessable value, its own rates deduction and its own 20% allowance. Aggregating them is named in the June 2026 report.

questions.q: A Hong Kong company carrying on business lets a property it owns. What relief is available from property tax?
options: It is exempt automatically with no application
It may apply for exemption, the income being chargeable to profits tax instead
It pays both property tax and profits tax with no relief
It pays property tax at 8.25%
questions.explain: Section 5(2)(a) allows a corporation carrying on a trade or business in Hong Kong to apply for exemption from property tax where the income is included in its profits tax computation. Without an application, property tax is charged and set off under s.25.

questions.q: A company pays property tax on a let property and the rental income is also assessed to profits tax. How is the property tax relieved?
options: Deducted as an expense in the profits tax computation
Refunded automatically
Set off against the profits tax payable
Carried forward as a tax credit indefinitely
questions.explain: Section 25 sets the property tax paid off against the profits tax payable. Separately, the property tax charged in the accounts must be added back in the computation - it is two adjustments in two places from one fact.

questions.q: On whom is property tax charged?
options: The tenant
The property manager
Whoever actually receives the rent
The owner
questions.explain: On the owner of the land or buildings, which includes a beneficial owner, a life tenant, a mortgagor in possession and a person holding under a Government lease.

questions.q: A lease grants two rent-free months at the start. How are those months treated?
options: Nothing is assessable for the rent-free months
The market rent is assessed for the rent-free months
The rent for the whole year is averaged across 12 months
The rent-free period is ignored and full rent assessed
questions.explain: No consideration is payable for those months, so nothing enters the assessable value. Including the rent-free period is named in the June 2026 report.

questions.q: A company lets a property and does not apply for the s.5(2)(a) property tax exemption. It reports the rental income in its profits tax computation as well. How does the tax actually payable work out?
options: Both property tax and profits tax in full, with no relief at all
Corporation profits tax at 8.25%/16.5%, with a full credit for the property tax already paid, so the tax on the rental profit is not duplicated
Only property tax; the profits tax return simply omits the rent
Only profits tax; property tax is waived automatically for companies
questions.explain: Property tax is charged in the ordinary way, and the rental profit is also brought into the profits tax computation (with the property tax itself added back as a disallowable expense), but s.25 then sets the property tax paid off against the profits tax payable, so the company is not really taxed twice on the same rent - it is simply an awkward two-step mechanism instead of a straightforward exemption.

questions.q: A let property's outgoings (rates paid by the owner, for example) exceed the rent receivable for the year. Can the resulting 'loss' be used anywhere in the property tax system itself?
options: Yes - the loss can be carried forward against future property tax
Yes - the loss can be set against the same owner's salaries tax
No - property tax has no concept of a loss; each property stands on its own and a negative net assessable value is simply nil
Yes - but only if the owner elects personal assessment for that year
questions.explain: Property tax simply has no loss concept - the 20% statutory allowance and owner's rates can reduce the assessable value to nil but never below it, and there is nothing to carry forward within property tax. The only route to any further relief is for the individual to elect personal assessment, which is a different tax mechanism entirely.

questions.q: A property is let to a relative at a nominal rent well below the market rate. On what value is property tax charged?
options: The token rent actually paid, however low
Nil - a nominal rent is treated as no consideration at all
Half of the market rent as a compromise
The market rent that would have been charged to an unconnected tenant, not the token rent actually paid
questions.explain: Section 5B(2A) charges the property tax on the consideration that would have been payable if the letting were at arm's length, where the actual rent is less than the market rent because of the relationship between the parties.

questions.q: A tenancy is renewed at a materially higher rent partway through the year. How is the assessable value affected?
options: As if a new letting had started - a fresh assessable value is set based on the new agreed rent from the renewal date
The original assessable value continues unchanged until the lease finally ends
No property tax is chargeable during the renewal negotiation period
The higher of the old and new rent is always used
questions.explain: The assessable value simply follows whatever consideration is actually payable for each part of the year - the old rent up to renewal, the new, higher rent from the renewal date - exactly as any change in the rent under the lease would be reflected.

questions.q: How does Government rent (as distinct from general rates) affect the property tax computation?
options: Government rent paid by the owner is deductible, just like rates
The government rent is not deductible by the owner, whether paid by the owner or the tenant
Government rent is only deductible if the property is a flat
Government rent is deducted before computing the assessable value, not after
questions.explain: Only rates paid by the owner are a specific deduction under s.5(1A). Government rent is not separately deductible at all - like mortgage interest and repair costs, it is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much is actually paid.

questions.q: A property let at $20,000 a month stood genuinely vacant, with no tenant and no rent receivable, for 2 months of the year. What is the property tax payable for the year?
questions.explain: No rent accrues for a period the property is genuinely vacant between tenancies, so the assessable value covers only the 10 months it was actually let: $20,000 × 10 = $200,000. Charging property tax on a full 12 months' notional rent, as if vacancy made no difference, is the error to avoid - property tax is not a tax on ownership, only on consideration actually receivable.

questions.q: A property let at $35,000 a month stood genuinely vacant, with no tenant and no rent receivable, for 3 months of the year. What is the property tax payable for the year?
questions.explain: No rent accrues for a period the property is genuinely vacant between tenancies, so the assessable value covers only the 9 months it was actually let: $35,000 × 9 = $315,000. Charging property tax on a full 12 months' notional rent, as if vacancy made no difference, is the error to avoid - property tax is not a tax on ownership, only on consideration actually receivable.

questions.q: Does it make any difference to the owner's property tax whether the tenant uses the property for a business, as a residence, or as a charity's office?
options: It has no bearing on property tax at all - property tax is a separate charge on the owner regardless of the tenant's own tax position
The owner's property tax is reduced if the tenant also pays salaries tax
Property tax is waived if the tenant is a charity
The owner must obtain the tenant's tax reference number before filing
questions.explain: None. Property tax is charged on the owner by reference to the rent receivable, entirely independent of what the tenant does with the property or the tenant's own tax status.

questions.q: What is personal assessment?
options: It is a fourth head of charge alongside the other three
It is a relief, not a separate head of charge
It is compulsory for anyone with more than one source of income
It applies automatically where it reduces tax
questions.explain: Personal assessment is an election that re-computes income already chargeable under the three heads at progressive rates after allowances. It never makes non-chargeable income chargeable, and it is never automatic.

questions.q: For which of the following can electing personal assessment produce no benefit at all?
options: A sole proprietor with a mortgaged let property
An individual partner with a share of a partnership loss
A taxpayer whose only income is employment income
A property owner paying mortgage interest
questions.explain: Salaries tax already applies progressive rates and personal allowances, so there is nothing for the election to unlock. Personal assessment helps only where there is property income or unincorporated business profit charged at the standard rate with no allowances.

questions.q: What is the age requirement for electing personal assessment?
options: 18 in all cases, with no exception
21, or 18 if married
There is no age requirement
18, or under 18 if both parents are dead
questions.explain: The elector must be 18 or over, or under that age if both parents are dead.

questions.q: What makes a person a 'temporary resident' for personal assessment?
options: More than 180 days in the year, or more than 300 days in two consecutive years including the year of election
More than 60 days in the year of assessment
More than 183 days in the year of assessment
At least 90 days in each of two consecutive years
questions.explain: Either limb suffices. Contrast 'ordinarily resident', which is a factual test about residing voluntarily and for a settled purpose with sufficient continuity - a permanent identity card is evidence of it, not the test.

questions.q: From the year of assessment 2018/19, how is the residence condition satisfied?
options: The elector or their spouse may satisfy the residence test
The elector must personally be ordinarily resident or a temporary resident
Only Hong Kong permanent residents may elect
There is no residence requirement
questions.explain: From 2018/19 the elector must qualify on their own residence. Up to 2017/18 a married person could rely on the spouse's status; that route is closed.

questions.q: From the year of assessment 2018/19, how may a married person elect for personal assessment?
options: The election must always be made by both spouses jointly
Only the higher-earning spouse may elect
Either spouse may elect separately, or they may elect jointly
Married persons cannot elect at all
questions.explain: The Inland Revenue (Amendment) (No. 9) Ordinance 2018 introduced separate election from YA 2018/19. Before that a joint election was mandatory where both had income, so one spouse could veto it.

questions.q: A couple are jointly assessed under salaries tax. How must any personal assessment election be made?
options: Either may still elect separately
Neither may elect
Only the spouse with the higher income may elect
The election must be made by them jointly
questions.explain: Where the couple is already jointly assessed under s.10(2), the personal assessment election must also be joint. They cannot split for one and not the other.

questions.q: Where a couple elect jointly, how is the total tax apportioned between them?
options: In the ratio of each spouse's reduced total income
Equally between them
In the ratio of their gross incomes
Entirely to the spouse with the higher income
questions.explain: In proportion to each spouse's reduced total income - after interest and concessionary deductions, not gross. Each then receives their own notice of assessment.

questions.q: By when must an election for personal assessment be made?
options: Within 1 year of the end of the year of assessment
The later of 2 years after the end of the year of assessment and 2 months after a notice of assessment
Within 6 months of the notice of assessment
Before the tax return for that year is filed
questions.explain: For YA 2026/27 that means not later than 31 March 2029, or two months after a notice of assessment or additional assessment, whichever is later.

questions.q: By when must an election for personal assessment be withdrawn?
options: Within 2 years of the end of the year of assessment
Within 1 month of the assessment
Within 6 months of the date the personal assessment is issued
At any time before the assessment becomes final
questions.explain: Six months, or such longer period as the Commissioner considers reasonable. Where the election was joint, the withdrawal must be joint too. After withdrawal the taxpayer may not elect again for that year without the Commissioner's agreement.

questions.q: A person eligible to elect for personal assessment dies before doing so. What happens to the right of election?
options: The right of election lapses on death
Only the Commissioner may elect on the deceased's behalf
The surviving spouse alone may elect
His executor has the same right of election
questions.explain: The executor has the same right over the deceased's total income as the deceased would have had.

questions.q: Which figures are aggregated to arrive at total income under personal assessment?
options: Net assessable value, net assessable income, and net assessable profits
Gross rent, gross salary and gross business receipts
Assessable value, assessable income and assessable profits
Only income charged at the standard rate
questions.explain: Property enters at net assessable value - after rates and the 20% allowance - employment at net assessable income, and business at net assessable profits after losses brought forward and donations already relieved. Bringing property in at gross rent is a reported error.

questions.q: How much interest on money borrowed to produce property income may be deducted under personal assessment?
options: Unlimited
Restricted to the net assessable value of that property
Restricted to $100,000
Restricted to 20% of the rent
questions.explain: Capped at the net assessable value of that individual property (Board of Review D51/04). The excess lapses; it cannot create or increase a loss. This is a different relief from home loan interest under ss.26E/26F, which is capped at $100,000 and relates to a dwelling the taxpayer occupies.

questions.q: Tax under personal assessment is the lower of the progressive rates on net chargeable income and what?
options: The standard rate on net chargeable income
The progressive rates on reduced total income
The standard rate on reduced total income
16.5% on assessable profits
questions.explain: The standard rate applies to reduced total income - before personal allowances. Applying it to net chargeable income uses the wrong base and understates the cap.

questions.q: Total income under personal assessment is $1,420,000, interest to produce property income is $0, and allowances total $145,000. What is the tax payable?
questions.explain: Reduced total income $1,420,000; less allowances = net chargeable income $1,275,000. Progressive rates give $198,750; the standard rate on reduced total income gives $213,000. The lower is $198,750.

questions.q: Total income under personal assessment is $1,058,400, interest to produce property income is $200,000, and allowances total $290,000. What is the tax payable?
questions.explain: Reduced total income $858,400; less allowances = net chargeable income $568,400. Progressive rates give $78,628; the standard rate on reduced total income gives $128,760. The lower is $78,628.

questions.q: Total income under personal assessment is $884,000, interest to produce property income is $42,000, and allowances total $145,000. What is the tax payable?
questions.explain: Reduced total income $842,000; less allowances = net chargeable income $697,000. Progressive rates give $100,490; the standard rate on reduced total income gives $126,300. The lower is $100,490.

questions.q: What is the effect of electing personal assessment on a sole proprietorship loss of the year?
options: It must be carried forward against future business profits only
It is lost
It can be set against the taxpayer's other income in the same year
It can be surrendered to a spouse only
questions.explain: This is one of the two main reasons to elect. Without the election the loss is stranded in the profits tax computation and merely carried forward; personal assessment lets it shelter current-year salary and property income.

questions.q: Can an offshore business loss be brought into a personal assessment computation?
options: It can be set against Hong Kong income in full
It can be set against Hong Kong income at 50%
It may be carried forward under personal assessment
It cannot be brought in - offshore profits were never chargeable
questions.explain: No. Personal assessment aggregates income chargeable under the three heads. Profits that were never chargeable bring no loss relief either - the rule cuts both ways.

questions.q: A taxpayer with substantial salary income also owns an unmortgaged let property. Is personal assessment likely to be beneficial?
options: No - the marginal progressive rate exceeds the standard rate
Yes - progressive rates are always lower
Yes - allowances always produce a saving
It makes no difference to the tax payable
questions.explain: Above roughly $200,000 of net chargeable income the marginal progressive rate is 17%, against a 15% standard rate. Aggregating the property income drags it up to 17%, and there is no mortgage interest or loss for the election to unlock. Compute both ways - never assume.

questions.q: Which of the following cannot elect for personal assessment?
options: A sole proprietor
A company
An individual partner
An individual with property income
questions.explain: Personal assessment is available to individuals only. A corporate partner is assessed on its share at corporate rates and that is the end of it.

questions.q: How must an election for personal assessment be made?
options: Orally, by telephoning the Inland Revenue Department
By simply paying the lower amount of tax
In writing, in the tax return or on Form IR76C
By ticking a box on the demand note
questions.explain: The election must be in writing - in practice by completing the relevant section of the tax return, or on Form IR76C.

questions.q: A married couple elect for personal assessment. What allowance may they claim between them for their marital status?
options: Both allowances in full, one after the other
Neither allowance, since personal assessment has its own separate scale
Half of each allowance
The higher of the two allowances - not both
questions.explain: The married person's allowance under personal assessment works the same way as under salaries tax - one married couple gets one married person's allowance (or, unmarried, each their own basic allowance), never both a basic and a married allowance stacked together.

questions.q: Are child, dependent parent, dependent sibling, and disability allowances available under a personal assessment computation?
options: Yes - each qualifying child allowance, dependent parent allowance and so on is available under personal assessment exactly as under salaries tax
No - personal assessment allows only the basic or married allowance, with no allowance for children or dependants
Only the child allowance is available; dependent parent and sibling allowances are not
Allowances are halved under personal assessment
questions.explain: The full suite of personal allowances under Part V (basic, married, child, dependent parent, dependent sibling, single parent, disabled dependant, personal disability) is available to reduce reduced total income to net chargeable income, exactly as in a salaries tax computation.

questions.q: Are the concessionary deductions available under salaries tax (self-education expenses, home loan interest, elderly residential care expenses, MPF contributions, approved charitable donations) also available under personal assessment?
options: No concessionary deductions are available under personal assessment
Yes - the same concessionary deductions (self-education expenses, home loan interest, MPF contributions, elderly residential care expenses, approved charitable donations, and so on) are all available
Only home loan interest is available; the others are salaries-tax only
Concessionary deductions are capped at half their normal limits under personal assessment
questions.explain: Yes, at the same statutory caps, deducted from total income before arriving at reduced total income - alongside the personal-assessment-specific deductions for business losses and interest to produce property income that salaries tax alone does not offer.

questions.q: Does electing personal assessment change how income from each individual source (property, employment, business) is itself computed?
options: Yes - personal assessment recomputes every source of income on a cash receipts basis
Only property income is recomputed; business profits keep their normal basis
No - each source of income keeps its own basis; property income is still computed on an accruals basis and business profits on the normal profits tax basis, merely aggregated afterwards
Personal assessment abolishes the concept of a basis period entirely
questions.explain: Personal assessment is purely a re-aggregation and re-rating mechanism. Each source's net assessable value, net assessable income or assessable profits is computed exactly as it would be under the ordinary property tax, salaries tax or profits tax rules, and only then are the results added together and taxed afresh.

questions.q: In which of the following is personal assessment LEAST likely to produce any tax saving?
options: A property is solely owned by one spouse and let for the whole year
A sole trader's business runs at a loss for the year
A taxpayer pays substantial home loan interest with little other income to absorb allowances
A property is jointly owned by a married couple; only the spouse who elects personal assessment includes their own share
questions.explain: Where a property is solely owned and let for the whole year with no mortgage, there is nothing for personal assessment to unlock - no loss to use, no interest to deduct beyond what property tax itself already sets off against rates, and the standard rate on that income alone is likely to beat the progressive computation once it is aggregated with other income. Always compute the tax both ways rather than assuming.

questions.q: In an exam question asking whether a married couple should elect for personal assessment, what should the answer actually compare?
options: The whole family's tax position, computed both with and without the election, for each spouse separately and jointly
Only the spouse with the higher income
The election is never worth comparing - it should always be made if available
Only the spouse who owns the let property
questions.explain: Compute the total family tax bill under each realistic combination - no election, each spouse electing separately, and a joint election - and recommend whichever gives the lowest total. There is no shortcut rule that always wins; election is a comparison exercise, not an automatic saving.

questions.q: A sole trader's business made a loss last year (say YA 2024/25), which was simply carried forward under the profits tax computation because no election was made at the time. Can personal assessment still be used now to relieve that loss against last year's other income?
options: The loss is forfeited once the year of assessment for the loss has passed
The loss is still relievable, since personal assessment for a year can be elected up to two years after that year ends
The loss must be relieved in the same year it is incurred or never at all
Only losses incurred in the current year of assessment qualify
questions.explain: The time limit for electing personal assessment for a given year runs for two years after that year of assessment ends (or longer following a late assessment), so there is still time to go back and elect for YA 2024/25 itself, setting that year's loss against that year's other income, rather than only being able to use the loss against future profits.

questions.q: In the personal assessment computation, what does 'total income' mean before it becomes 'reduced total income'?
options: It is the same thing as net chargeable income
It is total income after personal allowances only
It is the total income of the individual, before deducting interest, concessionary deductions or losses - the starting point of the computation
It is only the individual's salary income, excluding property and business income
questions.explain: Total income is simply the sum of the individual's net assessable value, net assessable income and assessable profits from all sources - the starting point, before any of the personal-assessment-specific deductions (interest, concessionary deductions, losses) are subtracted to arrive at reduced total income.

questions.q: An individual partner in a mixed partnership elects personal assessment. What happens to the corporate partner's share of the same partnership's profit?
options: It is excluded from the partnership computation entirely
It is halved
It is deferred until the corporate partner also elects personal assessment
It is included in full, since a corporate partner's own separate assessment is unaffected by what an individual partner elects
questions.explain: Each partner's share is assessed independently of what any other partner elects. The corporate partner's share of profit continues to be assessed under ordinary profits tax at the corporate rate, entirely unaffected by the individual partner's personal assessment election.

questions.q: Must a taxpayer have more than one source of chargeable income before personal assessment is worth considering?
options: Yes - a non-Hong Kong-sourced loss cannot be brought in, but Hong Kong-sourced property, employment and business income can all still be aggregated even where some of it individually would be modest
No - personal assessment requires at least two separate sources of chargeable income
No - personal assessment is only available where property income exists
Yes, but only where the taxpayer's total income exceeds $1,000,000
questions.explain: There is no such requirement in the legislation - even a taxpayer with a single source can elect - but as a matter of practical benefit, personal assessment tends only to help where there is property or business income (with a loss, or mortgage interest, or no allowances of its own) to combine with something else; a single salary source alone gains nothing from electing.

questions.q: What happens if an election for personal assessment is made after the statutory time limit in s.41(2) has passed?
options: A late election is always accepted with no discretion required
The Commissioner may refuse to accept a late election, though in practice a reasonable excuse for the delay is usually accommodated
A late election converts automatically into an objection instead
There is no consequence, since personal assessment has no time limit at all
questions.explain: The election is out of time and the Commissioner is not obliged to accept it, though there is administrative practice of accepting a late election where there is a reasonable explanation - it should never be assumed as of right.
